articles.body_html:
Intro

AI Avatar is a free app where your VRoid (VRM) avatar cheers you with all its might.🤗 It lives in your VS Code sidebar (reacts to Claude Code /Codex /GitHub Copilot) or browser side panel (reacts to ChatGPT / Claude). Animations and speech bubbles all run without AI too.

This time, I have 3 main topics.

  • AI Avatar Security
  • Voxel Avatar Update
  • AWS Clean Up

Let's check them out together!😆

AI Avatar Security

In Japan, unauthorized access and sensitive data leaks caused by hackers have increased dramatically since September. I heard that personal data records exceeding twice Japan's population have now been leaked. This security situation does not seem to be happening only in Japan but also around the world. It’s quite horrifying. I wonder if this is partly due to the development of AI.

I have been using AI at work and for fun every day for more than a year, and I know how much smarter it has become in a short time. So this time, I decided to add a security support feature called AI Avatar Security to AI Avatar.

I am not a security expert, and I made it to learn about security. But I hope this will be helpful to others too. I also hope it will motivate others to learn more about security incidents.

There are three main features in AI Avatar Security.

  • Security Check
  • AI Review
  • Security News

Security Check

In Security Check, there are two types of checks. A library vulnerability check and a data leakage check. The library vulnerability check uses npm audit to check for the known vulnerabilities. It lets you know which libraries have vulnerabilities. The data leakage check uses Betterleaks (formerly Gitleaks) to detect exposed keys and passwords.

Security is not such a fun thing, but I added avatar animations based on the check results and tried to make it a little more fun and motivating.

NG Animation

If there are any security issues, a virus-like animation is played. It doesn’t mean the app is infected with a virus.🦠 I added the animation to make security checks more fun.

OK Animation

If there are no problems, a shining animation is played. Let’s feel relieved that there are no problems.

AI Review

I added an AI prompt for security checks to help prevent unauthorized access and sensitive data leakage. I also added an option to add tests for them.

Category What AI checks
Unauthorized Access Login and authentication
Unauthorized Access Roles and permissions
Unauthorized Access Data between users and teams
Unauthorized Access Private files and downloads
Sensitive Data Leakage Keys and passwords
Sensitive Data Leakage Private data in responses
Sensitive Data Leakage Logs and error messages
Sensitive Data Leakage Public files and storage

You can scan all eight at once, but scanning just one at a time seemed to provide a deeper analysis.

Security News

I added a security news checker. It uses two sources:

CIS (Center for Internet Security) for software vulnerabilities, and

NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) for general security advice.

Please check the latest security news and update your security knowledge.

AWS Cleanup

By the way, I was also checking and improving my personal cybersecurity. I finally got off my butt and decided to clean up my AWS account. I was just stopping my services to avoid getting charged and wasn’t deleting them because I knew it would be so hard and take time.

Some of the services couldn’t be deleted all at once, and I needed to delete them one by one by entering their names. So I asked my AI to write code that could delete them all at once using CloudShell. First, I was deleting the services shown in CloudWatch logs, but soon I noticed that this didn’t cover all services. So next, I used Resource Explorer, enabled indexing in all regions, and checked which services I had used were still left. But default settings that didn’t need to be deleted also showed up. So I asked AI to scan and list only the services I had used. I finally deleted all the unnecessary services.

A few days later, I checked Cost Explorer and found that I had been charged a few dollars because deleting the services had triggered Config. I would have deleted the whole account if I had known it would be so hard and that I would even have to pay more.

However, I love using AWS because it is convenient and offers many services, so I would like to keep using it. But from now on, I will try to clean up regularly and avoid accumulating too many resources.

Voxel Avatar Update


Voxel Avatar is an idle game where you can grow a garden and place animals while using VS Code and the Chrome extension. My DEV friend @shubhradev gave me a great idea in my previous post, a winter version. Thank you for your idea! So I added a snow animation this time. It made the voxel world look completely different and fun. The Voxel Avatar feature has grown into one of the core features of AI Avatar, so I would like to update it even more.

How to Use the AI Avatar VS Code Extension Version (Thank you 400+ installs!)

You can download the AI Avatar VS Code extension in two ways.

  • Option 1: Install from VS Code: Extensions button in the left sidebar > Search AI Avatar > Install ↓↓

  • Option 2: Install from the VS Code Marketplace: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=web-developer-hyper.ai-avatar ↓↓

How to Use the AI Avatar Chrome Version

Install from Chrome Web Store: ↓↓
https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/ai-avatar/afmcfaeaaojalninahhhjnonhmlmiidi

Special Thanks

  • My DEV Community friend and CCO (Chief Creative Officer) 🤣, @annavi11arrea1 collaborated with Catbot and AI Avatar in version 17, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My friend and CDO (Chief Design Officer)🤣, @rutenveil helped create the cool effects in version 15. and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My DEV Community friend and CTO (Chief Technology Officer)🤣, @gramli helped update AI Avatar in version 2, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My DEV Community friend and CMO (Chief Marketing Officer)🤣, @itsugo. Our avatar collaboration project was the beginning of AI Avatar, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My colleague Maximum Blue helped make unique avatars in version, 6 and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!

Version 29 Update

I'm already working on the version 29 update. More fun updates, so please stay tuned!

Outro

Ah! It's time for a security check, so I have to go now.💨 I would love to add more fun features and also use the latest AI in my next updates. I hope you enjoy the new updates to AI Avatar. Thank you for reading, and have a wonderful AI Avatar life!

Comments Welcome!

  • Do you have any ideas for more helpful security checks?
  • Do you have any ideas to make AI Avatar even more fun?

  • Do you have any ideas for making cool avatars and animations?

Any other comments are also welcome!

articles.title: Give Your Voice Agent Hands: Let It Act Across Sales and Marketing
articles.description: The call ends. The admin starts.   Maya is an account executive. She just finished a good...
articles.body_html:
The call ends. The admin starts.

Maya is an account executive. She just finished a good call with Priya at Larkspur Freight. They agreed on pricing in principle, Priya wants a recap in writing, there's a follow-up on Tuesday, and Larkspur's CMO should hear about the enterprise plan.

Now Maya has fifteen minutes before her next call, and four tools to update:

  • HubSpot: log the call, move the deal to negotiation.
  • Apollo: find the CMO, add her as a contact, put her in the enterprise sequence.
  • Google Calendar: book Tuesday.
  • Gmail: write the pricing recap.

Her team already has a voice agent. It's good at talking. It can summarize the call and suggest next steps. But it can't touch any of those four tools, so Maya does all of it by hand, again.

The obvious fix is to give the agent access to those apps. With voice, that's harder than it sounds:

  • There's no screen mid-call. If HubSpot's connection expired, the agent can't pop up an OAuth consent page while Maya is talking to it.
  • Every tool slows the reply. Each tool schema goes into the model's context on every turn. In a chat app, a second of extra thinking is fine. In a voice call, it's an awkward silence.
  • Voice gets misheard. "Draft Priya the recap" can become "send Priya the recap." One wrong word and a half-finished email reaches a prospect.
  • Maya can't see what changed. In a chat UI she'd see the tool calls scroll by. On a call, she only knows what the agent tells her.

This article builds a voice agent that handles that whole list for one rep, with her own access, and tells her what it did.

The job: one sentence, five actions

Here's the job, in Maya's words:

When I hang up with a prospect, I want to say what happened and have the CRM, follow-up and outreach updated before my next call.

So after the call she says one thing:

"Log the Larkspur Freight call, move the deal to negotiation, book a follow-up for Tuesday, draft Priya the pricing recap, and add their CMO to the enterprise sequence."

That sentence turns into five actions, each backed by a tool from the connector's docs:

What Maya asked App Tools
Log the call, move the deal HubSpot hubspot_deals_search, hubspot_call_log, hubspot_deal_update
Find the CMO and add her to the sequence Apollo apollo_enrich_contact, apollo_create_contact, apollo_add_contacts_to_sequence
Book Tuesday's follow-up Google Calendar googlecalendar_create_event
Draft the pricing recap Gmail gmail_create_draft
Tell her what changed (the agent) none, it reads back what the tools returned

Two choices here are deliberate.

The recap is saved as a draft, not sent. gmail_create_draft exists next to gmail_send_message, and for a voice agent the draft is the right default. If a word was misheard, it sits in Maya's drafts folder instead of Priya's inbox.

And the agent reads back what it did: "Logged the call, moved Larkspur to Negotiation, booked Tuesday at 10, saved the recap as a draft, and added Dana Okafor to the enterprise sequence." On a voice call, that read-back is the only audit trail Maya sees.

Building it yourself

You can wire this up directly. Here's what that takes for a team of 30 reps.

Three OAuth apps, four tools. HubSpot, Apollo and Google each need an OAuth app, a consent flow, scopes, an encrypted token store per rep, and refresh logic. Google Calendar and Gmail can share one Google app, but their scopes still need to be right.

Token handling that works mid-call. A rep's HubSpot token expires at 2 p.m. The voice agent tries to log a call at 2:05 and fails. Your code needs to refresh before the call, and if refresh isn't possible, say so out loud and get a link to the rep somewhere other than the call.

A tool list small enough to talk with. The four connectors together expose hundreds of tools. HubSpot's connector alone has 457 in Scalekit's catalog, 80 of them destructive. You'll hand-pick eight, write their schemas, and keep them in sync as the APIs change.

Guardrails against mishearing. You'll need to make sure no delete, archive or send tool is reachable, however the request was transcribed.

A record of every action, per rep. When a deal moves stage and nobody remembers why, you need to know which rep's agent did it, when, and what came back.

None of that is hard on its own. Together it's the bulk of the project, and every new app and new rep makes it bigger. The voice part, it turns out, is the easy part.

Building it with Scalekit and Vapi

This version extends Scalekit's Vapi voice assistant cookbook, which shows the pattern with Google Calendar, to HubSpot, Apollo and Gmail. Vapi handles speech and the conversation. Scalekit sits between the agent and the apps: it holds each rep's connections, exposes only the tools this role needs, and logs every call.

Step 1: Each rep connects their apps once

Before Maya's first call, she connects HubSpot, Apollo and Google, for example from a settings page in your app. Your backend asks Scalekit for her connected account on each connection and, if it isn't active yet, gets an authorization link to send her:

import os
from scalekit import ScalekitClient

scalekit = ScalekitClient(
    env_url=os.environ["SCALEKIT_ENV_URL"],
    client_id=os.environ["SCALEKIT_CLIENT_ID"],
    client_secret=os.environ["SCALEKIT_CLIENT_SECRET"],
)
actions = scalekit.actions

# Use the connection names you created in the Scalekit dashboard
CONNECTIONS = ["hubspot", "apollo", "googlecalendar", "gmail"]

def links_needed(rep_id: str) -> dict:
    """Return an authorization link for every connection that isn't active."""
    links = {}
    for name in CONNECTIONS:
        account = actions.get_or_create_connected_account(
            connection_name=name, identifier=rep_id
        ).connected_account
        if account.status != "ACTIVE":
            links[name] = actions.get_authorization_link(
                connection_name=name, identifier=rep_id
            ).link
    return links

rep_id is your app's ID for Maya. Her tokens stay in Scalekit, encrypted, and get refreshed there. Neither your voice app nor the model ever sees them.

Step 2: A Virtual MCP server with only this role's tools

The four connectors expose hundreds of tools between them. Maya's agent gets eight. You define that once, as a Virtual MCP server for the role:

from scalekit.actions.models.mcp_config import McpConfigConnectionToolMapping as Tools

response = actions.mcp.create_config(
    name="ae-post-call",
    description="Post-call updates for account executives",
    connection_tool_mappings=[
        Tools(connection_name="hubspot", tools=[
            "hubspot_deals_search", "hubspot_call_log", "hubspot_deal_update",
        ]),
        Tools(connection_name="apollo", tools=[
            "apollo_enrich_contact", "apollo_create_contact",
            "apollo_add_contacts_to_sequence",
        ]),
        Tools(connection_name="googlecalendar", tools=["googlecalendar_create_event"]),
        Tools(connection_name="gmail", tools=["gmail_create_draft"]),
    ],
)
MCP_CONFIG_ID = response.config.id
MCP_SERVER_URL = response.config.mcp_server_url

Look at what's not on the list. None of HubSpot's 80 destructive tools, neither of Apollo's two (apollo_archive_sequence, apollo_remove_records_from_list), none of Google Calendar's six, and none of Gmail's eight delete and trash tools. gmail_send_message isn't there either. Whatever the transcription says, the agent can't delete, archive, remove or send. And eight schemas instead of hundreds keeps every turn short, which matters when someone is waiting for a spoken reply.

Step 3: Pass the rep's identity at the start of every call

When Maya taps "Start call," your backend checks her connections, then mints a session token for her on that server. The token is bound to her identifier, so every tool call in this conversation runs with her access and nobody else's.

from datetime import timedelta

@app.post("/api/voice/start")
def start_call(user=Depends(current_user)):
    rep_id = user.id  # from your own auth, never from the browser

    missing = links_needed(rep_id)
    if missing:
        notify_rep(rep_id, missing)  # e.g. Slack DM or email with the links
        return {"status": "reconnect", "apps": list(missing)}

    session = actions.mcp.create_session_token(
        mcp_config_id=MCP_CONFIG_ID,
        identifier=rep_id,
        expiry=timedelta(minutes=30),
    )
    return {
        "status": "ok",
        "scalekitToken": session.token,
        "sequenceId": user.team.enterprise_sequence_id,
        "mailboxId": user.apollo_mailbox_id,
    }

This is how a lapsed connection gets handled with no screen. If Maya's HubSpot grant has expired, the call doesn't start silently broken. Your app tells her which app to reconnect and sends the link to wherever she'll see it. If a connection lapses mid-call, the tool call fails, and the agent's instructions (Step 4) tell it to say so out loud rather than guess.

The session token lasts 30 minutes here (Scalekit allows 60 seconds to 24 hours). It can't be refreshed, so each call gets a new one.

Step 4: Point the Vapi assistant at the server

In Vapi, add an MCP tool to the assistant. Vapi's MCP tool takes a server URL and headers, and headers can use variables:

{
  "type": "mcp",
  "server": {
    "url": "<MCP_SERVER_URL>",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {{scalekitToken}}" }
  }
}

Then start the call from the browser with that rep's values:

const res = await fetch("/api/voice/start", { method: "POST" }).then((r) => r.json());

if (res.status === "reconnect") {
  showBanner(`Reconnect ${res.apps.join(", ")}. We've sent you a link.`);
} else {
  vapi.start(ASSISTANT_ID, {
    variableValues: {
      scalekitToken: res.scalekitToken,
      sequenceId: res.sequenceId,
      mailboxId: res.mailboxId,
    },
  });
}

Vapi discovers the eight tools when the call starts. The system prompt does the rest:

You help an account executive update their tools right after a sales call.
- Before writing anything, repeat back names, dates and the deal you found, and wait for a yes.
- Find the deal with hubspot_deals_search before updating it.
- Emails are always drafts. You cannot send email.
- Add contacts to sequence {{sequenceId}}, sending from mailbox {{mailboxId}}.
- If a tool says a connection needs to be re-authorized, say which app
  and tell the rep a reconnect link is on its way. Do not retry.
- When you're done, read back every change you made, one line each.

A note from the HubSpot docs: hubspot_call_log takes the call title, body, direction, duration and status. Check in the Scalekit playground how the logged call gets associated with the deal in your portal before you rely on it.

Step 5: Every action is logged against the rep

Every tool call goes through Scalekit, so each one is logged with the tool, the rep's identifier, timing and result. If Larkspur's deal stage looks wrong next week, you can see exactly which call moved it, from whose agent, and what HubSpot returned. Failures are marked as connector errors (HubSpot throttling, a scope it refused) or API errors (your setup).

Prefer LiveKit?

Scalekit's LiveKit cookbook does the same identifier hand-off a different way. Your server reads the signed-in user and passes the identifier in the agent's dispatch metadata, and the worker calls executeTool for each tool it defines. The cookbook notes that @livekit/agents 1.4.11 has no MCP toolset, so there you scope the tools by choosing which ones to wrap.

Both cookbooks have repos you can clone: Vapi and LiveKit.

When you don't need this

If the voice agent is for you alone, running on your own HubSpot and Google accounts, you can skip the integration layer. Put your API keys in environment variables, write the eight tools by hand, and you're done in an afternoon.

It starts to matter when the second rep wants their own access, when a connection expires mid-quarter, or when someone asks which agent moved a deal. That's when per-rep connections, a scoped tool list and per-call logs stop being nice to have.

Getting started

To try it with your own accounts, start with the Scalekit quickstart, then add the HubSpot, Apollo, Google Calendar and Gmail connections from the dashboard.

articles.title: Google Ads AI Tools: 7 Options Compared in 2026
articles.description: When a growth team runs paid search campaigns, the work splits into four jobs: strategy, creative,...
articles.body_html:
When a growth team runs paid search campaigns, the work splits into four jobs: strategy, creative, launch, and ongoing optimization. Most Google Ads AI tools handle one or two of those jobs. Some change bids. Some find wasted spend. Some generate assets. Others give you a workflow for launching and optimizing campaigns with a person still approving the decisions.

Choosing the wrong tool for your job means paying for features you do not use while the actual bottleneck stays in place. An agency managing dozens of client accounts has different needs from a solo founder running a single Google Search campaign. A creative team testing hundreds of ad variations needs something different from a PPC specialist who wants tighter budget controls.

According to Google's May 2025 announcement, its conversational Google Ads experience has been used by more than 500,000 advertisers to create Search campaigns. That adoption signals how normalized AI assistance has become in paid search, but it does not mean every tool does the same job or fits the same team.

In this article, we will compare seven Google Ads AI tools worth considering in 2026: Hellyeah, Google Ads AI, Optmyzr, Adalysis, Opteo, Adzooma, and AdCreative.ai.

TL;DR

The best Google Ads AI tool depends on whether you need native bidding automation, a managed paid media platform, agency-grade workflow controls, or ad creative generation.

  • Hellyeah: An AI-first growth platform for paid media, powered by the AIMA engine, that covers strategy, creative, campaign setup, launch, and continuous optimization across Google and Meta campaigns. A person approves every launch and optimization change. Best for founders, small businesses, and agencies that want campaigns operated for them rather than a dashboard of recommendations.
  • Google Ads AI: Native bidding and campaign automation built directly into Google Ads, including Smart Bidding and Performance Max. Best for advertisers who want to use native automation without adding another vendor and who already have a person managing account strategy.
  • Optmyzr: Rules, scripts, optimization workflows, and account-level alerts for agencies managing many Google Ads accounts. Best for PPC agencies with defined, repeatable processes they want to run consistently across clients.
  • Adalysis: Structured account audits, ad testing, and budget monitoring for PPC teams. Best for specialists who want a detailed diagnostic layer and a testing discipline in Google Ads.
  • Opteo: Prioritized recommendations and account monitoring for smaller teams. Best for solo managers and small advertisers who want a queue of explainable improvements without building a large rule library.
  • Adzooma: Account management, recommendations, and reporting through a simpler interface. Best for small accounts and first-pass account reviews where the alternative is doing no structured review at all.
  • AdCreative.ai: Image and copy variation generation for paid campaigns. Best for marketers who need more creative concepts and testable assets and have already established tracking and media strategy.

The main divide is between tools that automate one part of the campaign loop and platforms that operate the full workflow. Within each category, the differences come down to channel support, automation depth, and whether a human approves the output.

What Is a Google Ads AI Tool?

A Google Ads AI tool is software that uses machine learning or generative AI to handle part of the paid search workflow. That workflow spans several distinct jobs: deciding what to bid on, writing the ads, choosing who to target, monitoring performance, catching problems, and making adjustments.

Without any AI layer, every one of those jobs requires manual input. A campaign manager sets bids by hand, writes ad copy from scratch, monitors search terms in a spreadsheet, and adjusts budgets based on a weekly review. As the number of campaigns, accounts, or creative variants grows, that work expands faster than any one person can absorb.

A Google Ads AI tool takes on part of that load. Depending on the platform and configuration, it can provide:

  • Automated bidding: Adjust bids in real time toward a defined goal such as conversion volume or target return on ad spend.
  • Campaign creation: Generate keyword lists, ad copy, targeting parameters, and creative assets from a brief.
  • Performance monitoring: Surface budget anomalies, search term drift, and conversion drops before they cost significant spend.
  • Account audits: Check campaign structure, ad quality, and testing discipline against defined standards.
  • Creative generation: Produce image and copy variations for testing across ad formats.
  • Full campaign operation: Handle strategy, creative, launch, and optimization with human approval at key decision points.

The value of an AI layer increases as campaign complexity grows. A single campaign on a small budget may not need one. A production setup spanning multiple accounts, channels, and creative variants has a clearer case for automation.

How We Evaluated These Google Ads AI Tools

This comparison looks at how each tool fits into a real paid media workflow, with attention to both its automation capabilities and its operating model.

The main evaluation criteria are:

  • Ad network support: Which campaign types and channels does the tool actually support?
  • Automation depth: Does it automate bidding only, or creative, launch, and ongoing optimization as well?
  • Human approval model: Where does a person need to review and approve changes?
  • Agency vs. solo fit: Is the tool designed for one account or many?
  • Reporting and visibility: What can the user see about what the tool did and why?
  • Pricing model: How does cost scale with accounts, spend, or usage?

Each tool is evaluated against the job it is designed to do, not against every feature every team might want.

Quick Comparison: Google Ads AI Tools

Tool Category Best for Limitation Pricing
Hellyeah Managed paid media platform Founders and agencies that want execution plus oversight Built for Google and Meta today, with a smaller integration library than established players 5% of ad spend managed, no flat fee
Google Ads AI Native bidding and campaign automation Advertisers working inside Google Ads who want native automation Reporting and controls can feel opaque, especially in Performance Max Included with Google Ads
Optmyzr Rules, scripts, and optimization workflows Agencies managing many Google Ads accounts Requires setup and ongoing configuration to get value Paid, quote-based plans
Adalysis Audits, testing, and budget monitoring PPC teams that need granular QA Focused on Google Ads workflows rather than full campaign execution Paid plans
Opteo Recommendations and account monitoring Small teams that want suggested improvements Suggestions still need review and approval Paid plans
Adzooma Account management and recommendations Small advertisers seeking a simpler interface Less depth for complex multi-account operations Free and paid plans
AdCreative.ai Ad creative generation Teams producing many image and copy variations Creative output does not replace conversion tracking or media strategy Paid plans

Pricing figures reflect publicly available information as of November 2026 and can change. Verify current pricing on each provider's site before making a decision.

1. Hellyeah

Hellyeah is an AI-first growth platform for paid media. Its AIMA engine supports the full paid campaign workflow: strategy, creative production, campaign setup, launch, and continuous optimization across Google Search, Google Performance Max, Google Local Services Ads, and supported Meta objectives. A person approves every launch and every material optimization change before it goes live.

The platform is designed for two audiences. Agencies use Hellyeah to operate client campaigns with expert oversight, handling the work between a brief and a live, improving campaign. Founders and small businesses use it to run paid ads without assembling an in-house team or managing a separate ad agency relationship.

Hellyeah is a platform, not an agency. The distinction matters for how the workflow runs: the client retains visibility and approval authority, while Hellyeah's AIMA engine handles the execution layer. For signups or sales, conversion tracking needs to be connected. Lead campaigns can use Google's lead form and route leads directly into the Hellyeah dashboard.

Getting started

Create an account and connect your Google Ads and Meta ad accounts. Once accounts are linked, Hellyeah's AIMA engine analyzes the account history and generates a campaign strategy brief. A team member reviews the brief before any campaign is launched. For B2B teams using the managed track, onboarding includes a kickoff call to align on goals and conversion setup.

Key features

  • Campaign strategy: AIMA generates keyword research, audience targeting, and campaign structure recommendations from a brief.
  • Ad creative production: Copy and image assets are produced for each ad group and campaign objective, including Search and Performance Max formats.
  • Launch approval workflow: Every campaign launch goes through a human review step before it is submitted to Google or Meta.
  • Continuous optimization: AIMA monitors campaign performance and surfaces bid, budget, and copy recommendations on an ongoing basis.
  • Multi-channel support: Google Search, Google Performance Max, Google Local Services Ads, Meta Awareness, and Meta Instant Forms are all supported channels.
  • X-Ray analytics: Hellyeah's X-Ray product provides conversion tracking and performance analysis across connected accounts.

Limitations and trade-offs

Hellyeah is built for Google and Meta today. It does not support LinkedIn Ads, TikTok Ads, Demand Gen, Shopping, or Display campaigns yet. Teams that need cross-channel coverage beyond Google and Meta will find a smaller integration library than established players offer. The 5% fee model suits teams with active, ongoing spend more than those running low-volume experimental campaigns.

Pricing

5% of ad spend managed, with no flat monthly fee. B2C self-serve is available from a $50 balance. B2B managed service starts from $50K per month in managed spend. Both tracks run on the same 5% fee model.

Best for

Hellyeah is best for founders, small businesses, and agencies that need a paid media platform to handle the full operating loop: from strategy to live, improving campaigns. It is the right fit when the gap is execution rather than one specific feature.

Explore Hellyeah

2. Google Ads AI

Google Ads AI is the starting point because its native automation has direct access to auction-time signals that no third-party tool can replicate. Smart Bidding adjusts bids toward goals such as target CPA or target ROAS based on real-time signals including device, location, time, and audience membership. Performance Max automates delivery across all of Google's available inventory from a single campaign.

Google's own guidance reports that advertisers switching from target CPA to target ROAS see 14% more conversion value at a similar return on ad spend on average. That is a directional benchmark, not a guarantee. The result depends on clean conversion values, sufficient signal volume, and a campaign structure that matches the declared goal.

For advertisers who do not want to add another vendor, native AI is the lowest-friction starting point. The platform gives access to bidding automation, asset generation for Performance Max, and campaign recommendations without a separate subscription.

Getting started

Native Google Ads AI is available inside any active Google Ads account. Enable Smart Bidding by selecting a bid strategy such as Target CPA or Target ROAS when creating or editing a campaign. Performance Max campaigns are available as a campaign type. Google's conversational campaign creation experience is available for Search campaigns through the platform interface.

Key features

  • Smart Bidding: Real-time bid adjustments toward conversion, conversion value, clicks, or impression share targets.
  • Performance Max: Cross-inventory delivery across Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail, and Maps from a single campaign with asset-based optimization.
  • Responsive Search Ads: Multiple headlines and descriptions tested automatically to find top-performing combinations.
  • Campaign recommendations: Automated suggestions for budget, targeting, and ad improvements surfaced inside the interface.
  • Conversational campaign creation: Natural language input to generate Search campaigns, available for advertisers using the interface directly.

Limitations and trade-offs

The platform can obscure the reasoning behind recommendations and automated delivery decisions. Performance Max offers less manual placement and search query control than a tightly managed Search campaign. Teams that need granular visibility into what the system is doing, or who want to override specific automated decisions quickly, may find the native controls limiting. A person still needs to manage account structure, exclusions, conversion setup, and budget strategy.

Pricing

Included with Google Ads. There is no additional cost for native AI features. You pay only for ad spend.

Best for

Google Ads AI is best for advertisers who already have an account operator and reliable conversion tracking, and want to use native automation without adding a third-party vendor or subscription.

Explore Google Ads AI

3. Optmyzr

Optmyzr is designed around optimization rules, scripts, alerts, and account-level workflows. It is a strong fit when an agency has a known process and wants to run that process consistently across many Google Ads accounts without building the automation from scratch. The platform lets teams define rules, automate alerts, schedule reports, and run optimization workflows on a cadence they control.

Where native Google Ads automation makes decisions autonomously, Optmyzr puts the account manager in the loop. Rules trigger a recommendation or action that a person can review and approve. That model suits agencies that need auditability across client accounts and want to move fast without losing oversight.

The platform also includes tools for budget monitoring, search term analysis, Quality Score reporting, and campaign-level pacing. Agencies use it to replace the manual spreadsheet-and-script workflow that breaks down once the account count gets large enough.

Getting started

Connect Google Ads accounts through the Optmyzr interface using a Google MCC (My Client Center) link. Once accounts are connected, configure the rule library with your standard optimization logic. Optmyzr ships with a set of pre-built rules for common scenarios such as cost-per-conversion spikes, budget pacing, and search term review. Custom rules use a visual editor or JavaScript-style scripting.

Key features

  • Rule engine: Define optimization conditions, triggers, and actions that run on a schedule across connected accounts.
  • Shopping and search optimization: Tools for bid management, search term review, and Quality Score improvement.
  • Budget monitoring: Alerts and controls for campaign-level and account-level budget pacing.
  • Enhanced scripts: Write and deploy custom Google Ads scripts from within Optmyzr with version control.
  • Report builder: Automated client reporting with customizable templates and scheduled delivery.

Limitations and trade-offs

Optmyzr is not a replacement for strategy or account ownership. Teams still need to decide which rules are safe, validate conversion data, and review the changes the system surfaces. The platform requires meaningful setup time to get value: a rule library that is too permissive can automate the wrong decisions at scale. It is also primarily a Google Ads tool, with limited support for paid social workflows.

Pricing

Paid plans, generally quote-based. Pricing depends on the number of accounts and the features required.

Best for

Optmyzr is best for PPC agencies that have a defined optimization process and need to run it consistently across many client accounts. It is especially strong when the team can describe their process precisely enough to encode it as rules.

4. Adalysis

Adalysis focuses on account audits, ad testing, quality checks, and budget monitoring. It gives PPC teams a structured diagnostic layer around Google Ads: a way to find problems systematically rather than discovering them through a weekly manual review or a client complaint.

The platform is built around the idea that Google Ads accounts degrade over time without active testing and review. Ads stop being tested. Search terms drift. Budget pacing becomes irregular. Adalysis surfaces those issues through automated checks and a testing framework that enforces hypothesis, duration, and decision rules.

Where Optmyzr focuses on rules and workflows, Adalysis focuses on auditing what already exists and enforcing testing discipline going forward. The two tools solve adjacent but distinct problems.

Getting started

Connect a Google Ads account through the Adalysis interface. The platform runs an initial account audit automatically and surfaces issues across ad groups, search terms, budgets, and Quality Score. Set up ad tests by defining the test, control, and decision criteria. Alerts can be configured for budget anomalies, search term drift, and performance changes.

Key features

  • Account audits: Automated checks across campaign structure, ad quality, search term coverage, and budget use.
  • Ad testing framework: Structured A/B and multivariate ad tests with configurable decision rules and significance tracking.
  • Budget monitoring: Alerts for pacing anomalies, overspend, and underspend across campaigns and accounts.
  • Search term analysis: Tools for finding irrelevant queries, adding negatives, and monitoring query drift over time.
  • Quality Score reporting: Visibility into Quality Score components and trends across ad groups.

Limitations and trade-offs

Adalysis is a diagnostic and testing tool, not a full managed campaign service. Strategy, launch, and day-to-day decisions remain with the account operator. The platform is focused on Google Ads search workflows and is not designed for cross-channel campaign execution or paid social management.

Pricing

Paid plans.

Best for

Adalysis is best for PPC specialists and agencies who want a detailed audit and testing layer for Google Ads. It is most valuable when the account already has an operator who can act on the findings.

5. Opteo

Opteo turns account data into a prioritized queue of recommendations. Budget changes, keyword actions, ad improvements, and bid adjustments are surfaced in order of estimated impact. The interface is designed to be approachable for a small team or solo manager who wants guidance without building a rule library or managing a complex configuration.

Each recommendation comes with an explanation of why Opteo is surfacing it, an estimated impact, and a one-click apply option. Teams can review and apply improvements quickly without needing to diagnose the account from scratch. The tool connects directly to Google Ads and updates recommendations as account data changes.

Opteo works well as a middle ground between opening Google Ads directly and buying a full agency workflow platform. It does not replace strategic judgment, but it reduces the time spent finding issues that a more experienced account manager would catch in a routine review.

Getting started

Connect a Google Ads account through the Opteo interface using Google OAuth. Once connected, Opteo analyzes account history and generates an initial set of recommendations. New recommendations appear as account performance data changes. Apply recommendations individually from the queue or review them in context before deciding.

Key features

  • Recommendation queue: Prioritized list of account improvements ordered by estimated impact.
  • Budget monitoring: Alerts for overspend, underspend, and budget pacing across campaigns.
  • Bid management: Bid change recommendations based on performance trends and targets.
  • Ad testing: Basic A/B test management for comparing ad variants within ad groups.
  • Performance dashboards: Account-level and campaign-level views of key metrics with trend data.

Limitations and trade-offs

Recommendations still require human review and judgment before applying. Opteo is primarily a Google Ads recommendation layer and is not designed for cross-channel campaign management or complex multi-client workflows. Teams with many accounts or advanced rule requirements will find it less capable than Optmyzr or a full managed platform.

Pricing

Paid plans. Pricing is based on the number of accounts and monthly ad spend managed.

Best for

Opteo is best for small teams and solo managers who want a guided queue of improvement suggestions for Google Ads without the configuration overhead of a rule-based system.

6. Adzooma

Adzooma gives small advertisers a simpler interface for account monitoring, recommendations, and routine management. It is useful when Google Ads feels too dense for a new advertiser but a full managed service is not yet necessary. The free tier makes it accessible for teams evaluating whether a management layer will improve their process before committing to a paid tool.

The platform covers basic recommendations, budget tracking, performance reporting, and some automation features. Its value is in making the account more legible, not in providing the depth of a specialist audit tool or the rules engine of an agency platform.

Adzooma supports Google Ads, Microsoft Ads, and Meta Ads connections, giving small advertisers a single interface for monitoring across channels without paying for a multi-channel enterprise platform.

Getting started

Create an account and connect your Google Ads, Microsoft Ads, or Meta Ads accounts. The platform runs an initial account review and surfaces recommended improvements. A free tier is available that covers basic account monitoring and recommendations. Paid plans unlock additional automation and reporting features.

Key features

  • Recommendations engine: Automated suggestions for improving campaign performance across connected accounts.
  • Budget monitoring: Alerts for spend anomalies and budget pacing issues.
  • Performance reporting: Campaign and account-level dashboards with exportable reports.
  • Multi-platform support: Connections for Google Ads, Microsoft Ads, and Meta Ads from one interface.
  • Automation features: Basic rules and automated actions on paid plans.

Limitations and trade-offs

Adzooma has less depth for complex account structures, advanced testing, and high-volume agency operations than specialist tools like Optmyzr or Adalysis. Recommendations should still be verified against margins, lead quality, and the actual conversion action before applying. It is not a set-and-forget system.

Pricing

Free and paid plans. The free tier includes basic monitoring and recommendations. Paid plans unlock additional automation and reporting.

Best for

Adzooma is best for small accounts and first-pass account reviews where the alternative is doing no structured review at all. It is a sensible starting point for advertisers new to paid search automation.

Explore Adzooma

7. AdCreative.ai

AdCreative.ai generates image and copy variations for paid campaigns. It addresses the creative production bottleneck rather than bid strategy, account structure, or campaign operations. Teams use it to produce more testable assets than a designer and copywriter could create manually in the same time.

The platform connects to brand assets, generates variations based on defined formats and messaging, and outputs production-ready creative at volume. It is designed for teams that already know what they are testing but do not have the bandwidth to produce enough variants to run a meaningful test.

Creative generation is most useful when paired with a clear test plan. Producing more assets does not automatically produce more learning. Define the audience, offer, format, and success metric before generating dozens of variants, or the output adds volume without direction.

**Getting started

Connect brand assets, upload a color palette and logo, and define the ad formats needed. AdCreative.ai generates variations from the brand kit and any copy brief provided. Connect Google Ads or Meta Ads to pull in live campaign data and export generated assets directly to connected accounts.

Key features

  • Image generation: AI-produced ad images in multiple formats for Google Display and Meta placements.
  • Copy variation: Headline and description variants generated from a brief or existing top-performing copy.
  • Brand kit integration: Logo, color, and typography inputs that apply consistently across generated assets.
  • Performance scoring: A creative score assigned to each output based on predicted engagement.
  • Direct export: Assets exported to connected Google Ads or Meta Ads accounts.

Limitations and trade-offs

Generated assets do not tell you whether the offer is right, whether conversion tracking is working, or where budget should move. Creative generation is not a substitute for media strategy, audience research, or account management. The platform solves a production problem, not an optimization or operations problem.

Pricing

Paid plans. Pricing is based on the number of credits or assets generated per month.

Best for

AdCreative.ai is best for marketers who need more creative concepts and variations for testing and already have reliable tracking, a clear offer, and a media strategy in place.

Explore AdCreative.ai

How to Choose the Right Google Ads AI Tool

Choosing the right tool starts with naming the job you actually need done, not selecting the platform with the most features on a comparison page.

  • Are you missing execution or missing recommendations?

Most tools in this list surface recommendations and leave execution to the account team. If your problem is finding issues, tools like Adalysis, Opteo, or Optmyzr help. If your problem is not having the capacity to act on those issues and run campaigns end to end, Hellyeah addresses the execution gap.

  • Are you running one account or managing many?

A solo founder running one Google Ads account has different needs from an agency managing 50 client accounts. Optmyzr and Adalysis are built for multi-account management at agency scale. Opteo and Adzooma are simpler and better suited to smaller account footprints.

  • Which channels do you actually need?

Confirm that the tool supports the campaign types you run. Google Ads AI is limited to Google. Hellyeah covers Google and Meta. Adzooma supports Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Optmyzr and Adalysis focus primarily on Google Ads. AdCreative.ai exports to Google and Meta. Do not pay for a platform that cannot access the campaigns you care about.

  • Do you need creative at scale or optimization at scale?

Creative generation and campaign optimization are separate problems. AdCreative.ai solves creative volume. Optmyzr and Adalysis solve optimization discipline. Hellyeah addresses both within a managed platform workflow. Buying a creative tool when the actual bottleneck is bidding strategy will not move the number you care about.

  • What is your approval model?

Some teams want every change reviewed before it goes live. Others are comfortable with automated changes within defined guardrails. Hellyeah requires human approval for launches and optimization changes. Native Google Ads AI can make changes autonomously within the bid strategy parameters set. Optmyzr lets you define how much automation runs without review. Know your comfort level before choosing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the best AI tools for Google Ads?
The best tool depends on the job. Google Ads AI handles native bidding and delivery at no additional cost. Optmyzr fits agencies with repeatable optimization rules across many accounts. Adalysis fits PPC teams that need structured audits and ad testing. Opteo and Adzooma fit smaller teams that want guided recommendations. AdCreative.ai fits teams with a creative production bottleneck. Hellyeah fits teams that need the full paid campaign workflow operated with expert oversight.

Can AI run Google Ads without a human?
AI can automate bids, recommendations, asset creation, and parts of campaign management, but fully unattended operation is high risk. Conversion tracking can be wrong, budgets can move unexpectedly, and business context is rarely visible in account data alone. A safer model defines what can change automatically, logs every change, and requires a person to approve launches and material optimization decisions.

Is Hellyeah an AI tool for Google Ads?
Hellyeah is an AI-first growth platform for paid media, not a single-purpose Google Ads plugin. Its AIMA engine supports campaign strategy, creative production, launch, and ongoing optimization across Google Search, Performance Max, Google Local Services Ads, and supported Meta objectives. Pricing is 5% of managed ad spend with no flat fee. A person approves every launch and optimization change.

Are Google Ads AI tools worth paying for?
They can be worth paying for when repetitive work, account volume, or creative production is limiting results. Start by measuring the hours currently spent on the task the tool claims to automate. If the tool only adds another dashboard while tracking or offer quality remains weak, it is unlikely to create meaningful value. Match the tool to a defined operating problem before subscribing.

What is the difference between native Google Ads automation and a third-party tool?
Native Google Ads automation runs inside the auction with signals no outside tool can access. Third-party tools add workflow controls, audits, rules, or creative production on top of what Google provides. Neither replaces the other entirely. Most production accounts use both: native Smart Bidding for bid decisions, and a third-party tool for the management layer around it.

Final Thoughts

Google Ads AI tools have become a set of operating layers rather than a single category. The right stack depends on what part of the workflow is actually the bottleneck.

Start with native Google automation if you have an account operator and reliable conversion tracking. Add a focused tool when a specific gap appears: audits, rules, creative production, or guided recommendations. Choose Hellyeah when the gap is execution, and you need a paid media platform to handle the work from strategy to live, improving campaigns with expert oversight.

Before making a decision, verify current pricing, supported campaign types, and channel coverage at each provider's site. Features and pricing in this space change frequently.

articles.body_html:
Imagine an agency sharing a staging site with a client.

On Monday, the agency invites the client by email. On Friday, it removes them. The removal succeeds, but the client can still open the site.

Here is how that happens:

  1. The agency removes the client. The Durable Object holding the site's access list records the change immediately.
  2. The client's browser still has a signed Kinde token. The token remains valid until it expires. Kinde's default access token lifetime is 24 hours, and ending a session does not invalidate a token that has already been issued.
  3. A nearby data center has a cached copy of the access decision: this client may open the site. That copy is up to 30 seconds old.
  4. The client reloads the page. The gate finds the cached answer, trusts it, and grants access.

The token signature is valid. The cache is working as designed. The authorization decision is still wrong.

That is the problem I wanted to investigate with Wicket.

A signed token tells the gate who someone was when they authenticated. A cached access decision tells it what was true when that decision was last checked. Neither guarantees that the person is still authorized now.

Wicket is a small application that puts staging and preview sites behind an authentication gate. It runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses Kinde for authentication and billing. I built it to understand how authorization behaves when state is distributed across edge locations, and how long a revoked user can continue accessing a site.

The measurements in this article come from the deployed gate, tested against a real Kinde account from a laptop in Lagos. The Kinde outage test is simulated, which I explain in that section.

What Wicket does

Wicket puts a staging or preview site behind a sign-in page.

A Cloudflare Worker, which I call the gate, sits in front of the site. Visitors authenticate with an email address through Kinde. If the site owner has invited that email address, the gate forwards the request and attaches headers identifying the visitor. If the email is not on the access list, the gate refuses the request.

Site owners manage access from a dashboard or command-line tool. An invitation, which Wicket calls a grant, can also have an expiry time.

The owner's Kinde plan determines how many sites they can protect:

  • Free: 1 site
  • Pro: 10 sites
  • Business: unlimited sites

There are four kinds of state behind this workflow. They do not all have the same consistency requirements, so they cannot all use the same storage strategy.

State Where it lives How it changes
Kinde signing keys Memory, then the data center cache, then Kinde Rarely, when keys rotate
Site settings (address, open paths, mode) Memory, then Workers KV When the owner edits a site
Who may open a site One Durable Object per site On every invite, revoke, and expiry
Plan limit Kinde, read when a site is created When the customer changes plan

A Cloudflare Durable Object is an object with globally unique identity and strongly consistent storage. The other stores in this design hold copies or cached versions of data.

That distinction matters. Site settings can tolerate some propagation delay. A revocation needs a much stronger guarantee.

Verify the token without calling Kinde

The visitor's browser holds a Kinde ID token in a cookie. The gate verifies its signature, issuer, audience, and expiry locally using signing keys already held in memory.

It also rejects tokens issued more than an hour ago, even if their expiry time is still in the future. The reason is straightforward: the token establishes the visitor's identity, but I want that proof to be recent.

Kinde publishes its signing keys at:

https://<your_subdomain>.kinde.com/.well-known/jwks

Its documentation provides the JWKS endpoint, but does not specify how long an application should cache the keys or exactly how it should handle rotation. Those are implementation decisions I had to make.

Wicket uses three rules:

  • It refreshes the signing keys when the cached copy is older than 300 seconds.
  • If a token contains an unfamiliar key ID, the gate makes one new JWKS request. It limits these requests to one every 10 seconds, so an unknown or forged key ID cannot force a call to Kinde on every request.
  • If Kinde is unreachable, the gate continues using its existing keys for up to 24 hours.

There is also an important distinction between two failure states.

If the gate has no signing keys and cannot reach Kinde, it returns 503, not 401. A 401 tells the visitor their token is invalid and they should sign in again. But if the gate simply cannot obtain the keys needed to verify that token, it does not know whether the token is valid. Returning 503 represents that uncertainty more accurately.

Put access decisions somewhere strongly consistent

The most important question Wicket asks is:

May this email address open this site?

That answer needs to reflect invitations, removals, and grant expirations as quickly as possible. I store it in a Durable Object assigned to each site.

The gate asks the Durable Object for the decision. Memory and the data center cache sit in front of it to reduce the number of calls.

Workers KV is not suitable as the source of truth for this particular decision. Cloudflare documents KV as eventually consistent, with changes potentially taking 60 seconds or more to appear in other locations.

That delay is acceptable for site settings that rarely change. It is not acceptable for a revocation if the expectation is that removing someone should immediately stop access.

The cache layers still introduce a consistency problem, though. Each layer needs to know when the underlying answer was actually produced.

Wicket stores the timestamp returned by the Durable Object alongside the decision. It does not replace that timestamp with the time a cache entry was created.

This is easy to overlook.

Suppose a cache contains an authorization decision that is 20 seconds old. A Worker copies that answer into memory. If the Worker timestamps the memory entry with the current time, it now appears to be fresh for another five seconds. The memory layer might then refill from the data center cache, making the same old decision appear even newer.

The result is that copies can keep extending the life of an authorization decision without ever checking the source again.

By preserving the original timestamp, Wicket prevents that. An answer remains as old as the Durable Object's original decision, regardless of how many cache layers it passes through.

For a fast site, the cache windows are:

  • Worker memory: 5 seconds.
  • Data center cache: 30 seconds.
  • Negative decisions: 2 seconds in both layers.
  • Expiring grants: access stops at the grant's expiry time, even if a cached answer would otherwise remain valid.

Negative decisions have a shorter lifetime because the consequences are different. A stale yes can let a removed person in. A stale no can temporarily keep a newly invited person out.

A strict site skips both cache layers. Every request goes directly to the Durable Object.

How much does each tier cost?

I tested three sites on the deployed gate.

The first was a fast site receiving requests back to back. The second was another fast site, but it received one request every seven seconds. That interval is longer than the five-second memory window and shorter than the 30-second data center cache window. The third was a strict site receiving requests back to back.

For each request, the gate recorded which tier supplied the authorization decision and how long the request took from the laptop's perspective.

The network connection from Lagos accounted for roughly 200 ms before the gate did any work. A health page that skipped authorization entirely had a median response time of 200 ms.

Inside the gate, the median times were:

Tier Median time
Worker memory 0 ms
Data center cache 5 ms
Durable Object 8 ms

Two findings stood out.

First, the data center cache worked on a workers.dev address. It served 134 authorization decisions during the run.

Second, the cache was not faster at the tail. Its 95th percentile was 612 ms, compared with 235 ms for the Durable Object. In these runs, a cache hit avoided a Durable Object call but did not produce a better tail latency.

Memory was the only tier that was faster across every row. It is also the tier that disappears when a Worker instance is replaced.

This changed how I thought about the two site modes. The median latency difference between fast and strict was only 8 ms. The more important difference was how long a revoked user could continue getting access.

How long does a revocation take?

I wanted to measure that difference directly.

For each round, the test:

  1. Grants an email address access to a site.
  2. Makes four requests to confirm that the gate allows access.
  3. Revokes the grant.
  4. Sends another request every 100 ms until the gate refuses access.
  5. Measures the time between the revocation call returning and the first refusal.

I ran eight rounds against a strict site and eight against a fast site.

The results were clear.

The strict site refused the first request after the revocation. Its median wait was 0.21 seconds, and its longest wait was 0.24 seconds. That time represents one round trip.

The fast site took longer. Its median wait was 29.35 seconds, with the longest round taking 29.64 seconds. In every round, the last allowed decision came from the data center cache.

The 30-second cache window accounted for the entire delay. None of the runs exceeded it.

Cloudflare's Cache API documentation helps explain why Wicket cannot simply delete every cached copy after a revocation. Cache API entries are not replicated across data centers, and cache.delete only purges the cache in the data center where the Worker runs. A revocation in one location cannot directly remove copies held elsewhere.

That makes the cache window an explicit part of the product's authorization guarantee.

A fast site promises that a revocation will take effect within 30 seconds. A strict site promises that the next request will check the Durable Object directly.

The owner chooses the mode for each site. New sites use fast mode by default, while the command-line tool accepts --strict.

For sites where removing someone's access must take effect immediately, I would choose strict mode. Based on these measurements, the median cost was 8 ms.

What happens when Kinde is unreachable?

Kinde is needed during a request for one specific operation: retrieving the signing keys used to verify the visitor's token.

Wicket caches those keys for 300 seconds. Once that period passes, the gate attempts to refresh them. If Kinde is unavailable, the gate has to decide whether to keep trusting the existing keys or refuse requests.

Wicket uses both behaviours, depending on how old the keys are.

It continues using the cached keys up to a configured stale limit. After that, it returns 503. The default stale limit is 24 hours.

Owners can also designate paths as open. A health-check endpoint, for example, can skip authentication entirely, so a Kinde outage does not take that endpoint offline. Other paths fail closed once the signing keys exceed the allowed age.

I tested this behaviour on the deployed gate using a request header that makes the gate behave as though Kinde is unreachable for that request. The header can only simulate a failure; it cannot grant access. At the beginning of the test, the cached keys were seven seconds old, and I configured the stale limit to 60 seconds.

For the first 293 seconds, the gate continued returning 200 responses using keys from memory or the shared cache.

At 293 seconds, the cached copy became due for refresh. The gate then continued using the old keys for another 60 seconds.

The last 200 response arrived at 352 seconds. The first 503 arrived at 358 seconds. Requests were sent roughly every 5.5 seconds, so the refusal happened within one polling interval of the expected 353-second mark.

There was one detail I got wrong in my first attempt.

I initially treated the 60-second stale limit as though it started when the keys were first cached. But the gate does not check that limit while the copy is still within its 300-second refresh interval. It uses the existing copy without attempting a refresh.

The actual rule is therefore:

maximum key age = refresh interval + stale limit

With a 300-second refresh interval and a 60-second stale limit, the gate can use the keys for up to 360 seconds.

That distinction matters when configuring an outage policy. The stale limit does not represent the total age of the keys. It represents how long the gate will continue using them after a refresh becomes due.

Pass the visitor's identity to the protected site

Once the gate authorizes a visitor, the protected site needs a reliable way to identify them.

Wicket adds four headers to the forwarded request:

  • The site identifier.
  • The visitor's email address.
  • A timestamp.
  • A signature.

The signature uses HMAC-SHA256 and a secret shared between the gate and the protected site.

The protected site verifies the signature and rejects requests with timestamps more than 60 seconds old. Before forwarding the request, the gate also removes any incoming x-wicket- headers. That prevents a visitor from supplying their own identity headers and pretending to be someone else.

The protected site never receives the Kinde token and does not need to call Kinde. It only needs to verify the four headers using the shared secret.

Enforce plan limits where the count lives

Wicket also needs to enforce the number of sites an organization can protect.

It reads the protected_sites entitlement from Kinde's Management API when a site is created. The organization's Durable Object caches the plan limit for 30 seconds.

Kinde represents an unlimited feature with the value 2147483647. Wicket treats that value as unlimited rather than displaying it as a literal site allowance.

The important part is where the count and write happen.

Both operations run inside the same Durable Object, with no network call between checking the current count and creating the site. This means two simultaneous create requests cannot both pass a limit of one. The Durable Object processes them sequentially.

I ran into an unexpected issue while testing the plan limits.

After adding the protected_sites feature to the Pro plan, an organization that was already subscribed to Pro still reported zero of zero sites.

The reason was Kinde's plan versioning behaviour. When a plan is edited and published, existing subscribers remain on the version they originally joined. The updated entitlement applies to new subscribers.

To test the new limit, I had to move the organization off the plan and then subscribe it again. After that, Wicket reported zero of ten sites.

This is worth remembering when changing billing entitlements. Updating a plan does not necessarily update the entitlements of customers already subscribed to it.

Limits of these measurements

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results.

  • All timings came from one laptop in Lagos. The network round trip was roughly 200 ms before the gate did any work. That variation is larger than the difference between the authorization tiers. I did not choose where Cloudflare placed the Durable Object, so these results do not establish how that tier performs from other locations.
  • Each revocation result represents eight rounds. The fast-site measurements ranged from 29.17 to 29.64 seconds. That supports the 30-second cache window, but it does not tell us how the system behaves across many sites under load.
  • The Kinde outage was simulated. A request header made the gate behave as though Kinde were unavailable. The key-rotation behaviour was tested with a fake Kinde in unit tests, not through an actual key rotation on a live tenant.
  • Pausing a site has different consistency characteristics. Site settings are stored in Workers KV, so a pause can take the 60 seconds or more that Cloudflare documents for KV propagation. I measured revocations, which use Durable Objects. I did not measure site-pause propagation.

These measurements are useful for understanding the implementation and its trade-offs. They are not a global performance benchmark.

What I learned

An edge cache introduces multiple copies of the same authorization decision. Each copy needs a clear rule for how old it can be, and those rules need to survive when data moves between cache layers.

Three principles guided the implementation:

  1. Preserve the source timestamp. A cache refill must not make an old authorization decision look new.
  2. Set an explicit freshness window. That window determines how long a revoked user might retain access, so it is part of the product's security promise.
  3. Refuse requests when the decision is too old. Returning 503 when the gate cannot establish trust is safer than returning 200 based on an expired copy.

The most important design decision is the freshness window. It determines the maximum period during which a stale authorization decision can grant access.

For Wicket, that means a site owner has to choose between a 30-second revocation window and a direct Durable Object check on every request. The measured median difference was 8 ms, which makes strict mode a reasonable choice for sites where revocation speed matters more than avoiding that extra lookup.

Run it yourself

The source code is available in the Wicket repository.

You need a Cloudflare account and a Kinde account with billing enabled. Wicket is self-hosted: deploy the gate once, then manage protected sites through the command-line tool.

From the project directory:

npm install
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars

Add your Kinde machine-to-machine credentials, organization-to-customer mapping, and signing secret to .dev.vars.

Then run the tests and deploy:

npm test
npm run deploy

Before deployment, configure KINDE_DOMAIN and KINDE_CLIENT_ID in wrangler.toml, and add your organizations to public/config.js.

In Kinde, create a numeric feature with the code protected_sites on your plans. Add the gate's /_wicket/callback and /app URLs as callback URLs.

Upload the four required secrets using npx wrangler secret put, once for each:

  • KINDE_M2M_CLIENT_ID
  • KINDE_M2M_CLIENT_SECRET
  • CUSTOMERS_JSON
  • SIGNING_SECRET

Sign in through the command-line tool and protect a site:

npx wicket-gate login org_xxxx --url https://your-gate.workers.dev
npx wicket-gate protect https://your-staging-site.example --name preview

The repository includes scripts for repeating the measurements. Each script needs room for two sites because it creates and removes its own test sites.

Script What it measures
node scripts/tiers.mjs Round-trip latency and time spent in each authorization tier. Add --long for a longer run.
node scripts/revoke.mjs 8 Eight revocation rounds against fast and strict sites.
node scripts/kinde-down.mjs 60 Simulated Kinde outage with a 60-second stale limit.
node scripts/local-e2e.mjs End-to-end gate checks against a fake Kinde instance on your computer.

The steps for the local end-to-end test are documented at the top of its script.

FAQ

Why not put the access list in the token?

A token is signed when the visitor authenticates and remains valid until it expires. Kinde's default access token lifetime is 24 hours, and ending a session does not shorten an already-issued token's lifetime. An access list inside the token would become stale in exactly the same way.

Why not delete the cached copy after revoking someone?

Cloudflare's cache.delete only purges the cache in the data center where the Worker runs. Other data centers can still hold their own copies. The cache window provides the bound on how long those copies can be trusted.

Why does a negative decision expire after two seconds while a positive decision expires after 30?

A stale positive decision can let someone who has been removed continue accessing a site. A stale negative decision can temporarily prevent someone who has just been invited from getting in. The second mistake is less costly, so Wicket expires negative decisions sooner.

Why use a Durable Object instead of Workers KV for the access list?

Workers KV is eventually consistent, and Cloudflare documents that updates can take 60 seconds or more to reach other locations. A Durable Object provides strongly consistent storage for the access decision.

What happens if the gate cannot reach Kinde?

It continues using its cached signing keys. Once the keys are older than the refresh interval plus the configured stale limit, the gate returns 503. Open paths continue working because they skip authentication.

Does a signed token prove that someone still has access?

No. It proves the visitor's identity at the time the token was issued. Wicket checks current authorization separately, using the freshest access decision that is still inside its configured window.

Why does the stale limit start when a refresh is due?

The gate uses a cached copy without checking the stale limit while it is still inside the normal refresh interval. The stale limit only applies after that interval has elapsed.

Sources
