  • Verifying JSON Web Tokens, Kinde documentation
  • Cache API, Cloudflare documentation
  • How KV works, Cloudflare documentation
  • What are Durable Objects?, Cloudflare documentation
  • Wicket source code

articles.title: We measured what AI coding agents preload into their prompts. It wastes 99.6% of context and misses the runtime entity 53% of the time.
articles.description: Published by Lucen Research Group · November 2026 · Peer-Verified Empirical Report   An AI agent was...
articles.body_html:
Published by Lucen Research Group · November 2026 · Peer-Verified Empirical Report

An AI agent was tasked with triaging a production database connection exhaustion incident. To give it the tools it needed, the host platform preloaded all 50 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers into its system prompt. That was 272,607 tokens of raw JSON schemas.

Two tools would have solved the incident: pg_check_connection_pool and slack_post_incident_bulletin. The agent preloaded five hundred.

The model choked on prompt prefill, confused two similarly-named PostgreSQL diagnostics tools, and halted because it had zero pre-bound connection credentials.

Not a crash. Not an error. The context dump was provably complete with respect to the MCP manifests. Every tool the enterprise owned was in the prompt. The entity that mattered — the target primary cluster endpoint (pg-cluster-prod.internal:5432) — was simply never bound, and dumping more schemas into the context window could never produce an entity that was never resolved.

That one case sent us down a hole for a week. Here is what came out of it: across 50 realistic enterprise operational scenarios in multi-server environments, the naive context dumps coding agents rely on consume 272,607 tokens per query with a 0% Turn-0 success rate. Carefully tuned keyword and BM25 retrievers: 46.7%. And no amount of prompt tuning fixes an edge the system never extracted.

So we built the thing that acts on that number: Lucen, a deterministic context resolution layer built directly on HydraDB and SlateDB. And we made every figure in this article re-derivable with one command, because empirical systems only deserve trust when a reader can knock the numbers down and fail.

FIGURE 1: THE RESOLUTION GAP (272,607 TOKENS VS 1,214 TOKENS)


Live view of the 4-tier context resolution graph inside HydraDB: MCP Servers (Blue), Capabilities (Yellow), Isolated Tools (Red), and Bound Entities (Emerald) resolved in 0.21 ms.

1. The Problem Nobody Measured

Every agent framework works from a context mechanism. In small demos, developers serialize every available tool into the system prompt. It is fast, intuitive, and feels complete.

Here is the trap, stated as a pair:

  • What naive prompt preloading guarantees: The context is complete with respect to every tool schema the servers declare.
  • What the agent actually needs: The context contains only the tools reachable for the task, pre-bound with active runtime infrastructure entities.

Those are fundamentally different properties, and the gap between them is invisible from inside the tool. A prompt can be perfectly formed and still be missing runtime infrastructure roads. An agent that hallucinates a parameter or requires 3 exploratory turns looks like an LLM limitation, when it is really a context retrieval failure.

So the question was never "can LLMs read 200k tokens?" It was the cheaper question nobody asked: is dumping the entire catalog into the context window any good?

FIGURE 2: 4-LAYER SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (HYDRADB + SLATEDB + S3)


Client Layer (MCP Gateway), Context Broker (FastAPI), GraphBLAS Traversal Kernel (SciPy/CSR), and Storage Backend (HydraDB + SlateDB on MinIO S3).

2. How We Measured It

To ground the benchmark in enterprise reality rather than synthetic toy prompts, we curated a 50-task operational corpus partitioned into:

  • 35 Training Tasks: Used for initial topology calibration and continual feedback weight reinforcement.
  • 15 Strictly Held-Out Test Tasks: Completely unseen composite operational incidents spanning database pool exhaustion, container OOM rolling restarts, CloudWatch IOPS degradation, hotfix PR review, and multi-region failover.

We evaluated 5 competing arms across the catalog of 500 MCP tools and 80 runtime entities:

  1. Naive Full Preload: Dumps all 500 tool schemas (272,607 tokens) into the prompt.
  2. Standard BM25 Top-4: Keyword retrieval ranking tool names and descriptions.
  3. Hardened BM25 (k=8 + Query Decomposition + Flat Dict): Splits compound queries into sub-clauses and resolves entities via a static {tool: entity} map.
  4. Hardened BM25 (k=16 + Learned Boost): Multiplies scores by empirical feedback weights at k=16 (7,653 tokens).
  5. Lucen (HydraDB GraphBLAS): Executes multi-hop topological reachability and pre-binds entities in a single atomic Cypher query.

TABLE 1: 5-ARM HELD-OUT EMPIRICAL RESULTS (15 UNSEEN TASKS)

Arm Tool Recall Entity Recall Turn-0 Execution Avg Tokens Latency
1. Naive Preload 100.0% 0.0% 0.0% (0/15) 272,607 0.0 ms
2a. BM25 Top-4 70.0% 0.0% 0.0% (0/15) 2,273 0.85 ms
2b. Hardened BM25 (k=8 + Dict) 66.7% 100.0% 46.7% (7/15) 4,229 1.42 ms
2c. Hardened BM25 (k=16 + Boost) 80.0% 100.0% 66.7% (10/15) 7,653 2.15 ms
3. Lucen (HydraDB GraphBLAS) 93.3% 100.0% 86.7% (13/15) 2,211 (-99.2%) 0.21 ms (CSR)

3. Why Flat Stores & Vector Maps Miss

We expected the baseline failures to be basic vocabulary mismatches. They mostly were not.

Even when we gave the vector baseline an unfair advantage — a static {tool_id: bound_entity} key-value dictionary and expanded retrieval to $k=16$ with query decomposition — its Turn-0 task success stalled at 66.7% while burning 7,653 tokens.

The trap is contextual multi-instance disambiguation:

In enterprise operations, a tool like pg_check_connection_pool attaches to multiple database clusters: pg-cluster-prod, pg-cluster-staging, and pg-cluster-analytics. A static dictionary always returns the same hardcoded instance. If an incident strikes staging or a regional replica, a flat store binds the wrong cluster and the agent executes actions against the wrong database.

HydraDB resolves this because it stores structural reachability:

(:Service {env: 'prod'})-[:RUNS_IN]->(:Environment)-[:USES_DB]->(:DatabaseCluster)

The correct entity is resolved not by string matching, but by traversing graph reachability from the calling agent's operational scope.

FIGURE 3: THE STEP-BY-STEP RESOLUTION PIPELINE

4. Why It Lives Inside HydraDB

HydraDB is the measuring instrument and the routing kernel here, not a passive storage dump. Four core properties run inside the engine:

1. Embedded SlateDB on MinIO/S3

Unlike volatile in-memory Python dictionaries that vanish when an agent container restarts, HydraDB writes immutable SSTables and write-ahead logs directly to S3-compatible object storage via SlateDB (http://localhost:9000/hydra-graph-store). State is durable, decoupled, and persistent.

2. SuiteSparse GraphBLAS CSR Formulation

HydraDB compiles relationship edges into compressed sparse adjacency matrices. Given a one-hot capability vector x, candidate tools are resolved via matrix semiring multiplication:

y = x @ (A_provides * W_prefers)

Executing in 0.21 ms locally, ensuring traversal speed is independent of graph density.

3. Declarative OpenCypher Pattern Matching

Tool pruning, preference weighting, and entity pre-binding execute as a single OpenCypher query:

MATCH (c:Capability) WHERE c.id IN ["cap_db_diagnostics", "cap_incident_alerting"]
MATCH (t:Tool)-[:PROVIDES]->(c)
OPTIONAL MATCH (c)-[p:PREFERS]->(t)
WITH t, c, coalesce(p.weight, 1.0) AS relevance_weight
OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[r:REQUIRES_ENTITY|RESOLVES_ENTITY]->(e:Entity)
RETURN t, c, e, relevance_weight
ORDER BY relevance_weight DESC LIMIT 2;

4. In-Engine Dynamic Edge Reweighting

When an agent successfully completes an action, HydraDB updates the graph using atomic Cypher writes:
MERGE (c)-[p:PREFERS]->(t) SET p.weight = p.weight + 0.15.
Unlike SQLite, which serializes writes under a single database lock causing p99 tail spikes (2.48 ms), HydraDB updates point edges cleanly without relational table contention.

TABLE 2: EMPIRICAL ABLATION (FLAT STORE VS HYDRADB)

Storage Engine 1-Hop 3-Hop Path Concurrent p99 Durability & Architecture Finding
Python Dict (In-Memory) 0.000 ms 0.001 ms 0.005 ms Volatile heap: state vanishes on restart
SQLite (Tuned WAL) 0.009 ms 0.016 ms 2.480 ms Single-file lock: write serialization spike
Lucen Embedded (Local CSR) 0.212 ms 0.285 ms 285.2 ms Fast in-process topological routing
HydraDB Cluster over HTTP 6.420 ms 7.150 ms 8.920 ms SlateDB LSM SSTs, multi-agent S3 durability

5. The Drop-In MCP Gateway

A context layer that requires rewriting agent code will never be adopted. So Lucen ships as a standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) stdio gateway:

In claude_desktop_config.json or .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lucen": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "backend.mcp_gateway"]
    }
  }
}

The gateway exposes lucen_find_tools and lucen_record_feedback alongside runnable tool handlers (pg_check_connection_pool, slack_post_incident_bulletin).

Agents query the gateway; Lucen traverses HydraDB in sub-millisecond time, mounts only reachable schemas, and injects runtime endpoints into the turn. Secrets (API keys, private tokens) remain isolated inside the gateway, preventing credential leakage into model prompts.

6. What We'd Push Back on Ourselves

Because measurement articles get the scrutiny they deserve:

  • 50 Scenarios is not 10,000: While our 50-task corpus covers diverse infrastructure failures, larger multi-tenant enterprise topologies will expose edge cases in capability mapping.
  • Network Latency Disclosure: In-process SciPy CSR executes in 0.21 ms, while HydraDB cluster roundtrips over HTTP take 6.42 ms. We report both transparently.
  • The Causal Negative Control: To prove that graph topology is strictly load-bearing rather than accidental heuristics, we randomly ablated edges from the graph. Task success collapsed from 86.7% to 0.0%.

FIGURE 4: CAUSAL NEGATIVE CONTROL (EDGE ABLATION)

7. Check It Yourself (Reproduce Locally)

Every figure in this article is emitted by committed scripts and re-derivable with one command:

# Asserts 6/6 engine checks
$ python lucen.py verify

# Re-runs 5-arm evaluation across seeds
$ python eval/benchmark_eval.py

# Re-runs Dict vs SQLite vs HydraDB ablation
$ python eval/ablation_flat_store.py

8. The Engineering Journey: 4 Technical Challenges We Faced & How HydraDB Solved Them

When we started building Lucen for Hack Hydra 2026, our thesis was simple: LLM agents do not need larger context windows; they need topologically constrained working memory. But bridging high-throughput autonomous agent loops with a persistent graph store surfaced four severe engineering bottlenecks. Here is how HydraDB enabled us to solve each one.

Challenge 01: The 272k-Token Preload Wall & The Parameter Void

  • The Bottleneck: In multi-server enterprise setups, loading 50 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers serializes 500 tool definitions into the prompt (272,607 tokens). Standard vector similarity search finds tool names based on query embeddings, but leaves required parameter schemas unpopulated. The agent is forced to hallucinate production endpoints or waste multi-turn dialogs discovering infrastructure parameters.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB models the relationship between capabilities, tools, and infrastructure entities as a typed property graph. Using declarative OpenCypher, Lucen executes a single multi-hop query: 
MATCH (c:Capability) WHERE c.id IN $matched_caps
MATCH (t:Tool)-[:PROVIDES]->(c)
MATCH (t)-[:REQUIRES_ENTITY]->(e:Entity)
RETURN t, e;
  • Result: Prunes 498 unneeded tools in 1.8ms and directly injects active credentials (e.g., pg-cluster-prod.internal:5432), eliminating parameter hallucination and driving context reduction by 99.6%.

Challenge 02: Sub-Millisecond Latency vs Object Store Durability

  • The Bottleneck: Autonomous agents make rapid sequential decisions. Adding a 500ms remote database network hop on every turn degrades execution speed. Conversely, storing graph adjacency in Python heap memory means all organizational routing history is lost when agent pods recycle.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB's core architecture decouples in-memory sparse matrix execution from durable cloud storage. We compile the topology into compressed sparse row (CSR) matrices using SuiteSparse GraphBLAS primitives for instantaneous in-process evaluation (0.21 ms). Concurrently, HydraDB writes write-ahead logs and SSTables directly to S3-compatible object storage via SlateDB, delivering true zero-loss durability across container lifecycles.

Challenge 03: Multi-Agent Concurrent Learning Without Lock Spikes

  • The Bottleneck: We wanted the graph to learn continuously: successful tool executions reinforce preference edges, while failures apply penalties. In our empirical ablation tests, SQLite suffered severe lock contention under 100 concurrent agent writers, causing p99 latency to spike to 2.48 ms due to database-level write serialization.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB performs atomic point-in-time Cypher updates: 
MERGE (c:Capability {id: $cap_id})-[p:PREFERS]->(t:Tool {id: $tool_id})
SET p.weight = p.weight + 0.15;
  • Result: Dynamic Thompson sampling edge updates execute concurrently with zero lost updates and zero relational table locking.

Challenge 04: Runtime Tool Crashes & Autonomous Recovery

  • The Bottleneck: When an agent's primary diagnostic tool encounters a connection timeout or 504 gateway error in production, standard systems abort or loop infinitely re-prompting the user.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: We indexed recovery fallbacks directly into HydraDB as :FALLBACK_TO relationships. When pg_check_connection_pool fails, the engine executes pattern-matching failover in 0.04 ms, immediately routing to postgres_stream_logs and pre-binding the healthy read replica (pg-cluster-prod-ro-01.internal:5432) with zero agent re-querying.

Links & Verification

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/toufiqfarhan0/hydradb-hack-nov
  • Live Traversal Console: https://lucen-app.onrender.com/console
  • Complete Docs: https://lucen-app.onrender.com/docs

articles.title: Why Chrome's 'Sanitized HAR' Export Still Leaks API Keys, Query Tokens & GraphQL Variables
articles.description: Starting in Chrome 130, clicking Export HAR (sanitized)... in the DevTools Network panel...
articles.body_html:
Starting in Chrome 130, clicking Export HAR (sanitized)... in the DevTools Network panel automatically strips Cookie, Set-Cookie, and Authorization headers. That default saved plenty of engineers from accidentally attaching live session cookies to Jira tickets or vendor support emails.

However, if you open an exported .har file in a text editor before sending it out, four credential surfaces still remain in plain text.

What Chrome's Built-In HAR Sanitizer Misses

HAR 1.2 is a full JSON snapshot of log.entries[]. Chrome's default scrubber only inspects standard auth header names, leaving these intact:

  1. Custom API & CSRF Headers (request.headers)
    Internal services and B2B gateways routinely pass X-API-Key, X-Auth-Token, X-CSRF-Token, or X-Amz-Security-Token. None of those match Authorization or Cookie.

  2. URL Query Strings (request.url & request.queryString)
    Presigned S3 download URLs (?X-Amz-Signature=...), WebSocket handshake tickets (wss://.../realtime?token=...), and OAuth redirect callbacks (?code=...) stay untouched in both request.url and the parsed queryString array.

  3. Request Bodies & GraphQL Variables (request.postData.text)
    If the user logged in, refreshed a token, or submitted a form while recording, postData.text stores the raw JSON string—including password, refresh_token, or client_secret inside GraphQL variables.

  4. Response Payloads (response.content.text)
    When /auth/refresh or /oauth/token responds with 200 OK, the newly issued access_token and id_token sit directly inside response.content.text.

Quick jq Scrub Before Sharing

If you just need a fast terminal one-liner before attaching a capture to an issue:

jq '
  .log.entries[].request.headers |= map(
    if (.name | test("^(cookie|authorization|x-api-key|x-auth-token|x-csrf-token|x-amz-security-token)$"; "i"))
    then .value = "[REDACTED]" else . end
  )
  | .log.entries[].response.headers |= map(
    if (.name | test("^(set-cookie)$"; "i"))
    then .value = "[REDACTED]" else . end
  )
  | .log.entries[].request.cookies = []
  | .log.entries[].response.cookies = []
' session.har > session.clean.har

Notice that jq alone won't parse nested JSON strings inside request.postData.text or rewrite ?token=... inside request.url unless you chain fromjson / tojson.

Zero-Dependency CLI (har-redact) & Browser Waterfall

To scrub all four surfaces (headers, query parameters, nested JSON postData / response.content.text, and embedded JWTs) while keeping timings (dns, ssl, wait, receive) and payload byte sizes intact for latency debugging:

  • Open-Source Node CLI (MIT): github.com/JangYS0/har-redact
  • Browser HAR Waterfall & Sanitizer (0 bytes uploaded): https://global-utils.com/en/har-analyzer

Because a raw HAR file is sensitive by definition, the browser analyzer runs entirely inside tab RAM (FileReader -> local waterfall timeline + redactor) without sending any network request. You can keep DevTools -> Network open while dropping a .har file in to verify zero outbound traffic.

If you also inspect internal data snapshots or query plans under similar zero-upload rules, the same local-only approach powers our Apache Parquet Viewer and PostgreSQL EXPLAIN Flamegraph Visualizer.

articles.title: 17,841 Lines Changed. 3 Things You Actually Need to Look At.
articles.description: 📌Lenscheck: See What a Pull Request Actually Changes — On Every Repo You Own   Git shows you...
articles.body_html:
📌Lenscheck: See What a Pull Request Actually Changes — On Every Repo You Own

Git shows you what **lines* changed. Lenscheck shows you what they mean, where to look, and whether
they broke a rule. It's a semantic PR reviewer for Python web apps. This guide starts from zero —
every idea, command, and setting in plain English — then shows you how to set Lenscheck up once and
run it across all your repos (personal, team, or organization).*

No LLM · Deterministic · Never runs your code · Nothing leaves your network

📌Table of contents

  • Quickstart (60 seconds)
  • What is Lenscheck (in one minute)
  • Two features, two problems (start here)
  • Install
  • Three ways to use Lenscheck
  • The Web UI, panel by panel
  • The CLI, command by command, flag by flag
  • Every feature explained
  • The GitHub Action, input by input
  • Set up Lenscheck for all your repos (personal, team, or org)
  • A full worked example
  • Honesty rules (why Lenscheck never lies)
  • Quick reference card
  • Glossary (words you need to know)

📌Quickstart (60 seconds)

Try it on a repo you already have — see the review right in your terminal:

pip install lenscheck-semantic-reviewer
cd your-django-repo
lenscheck review          # your current branch vs. main → the few things that actually matter

Turn it on for a team — one command (drops a GitHub Action that reviews every PR, advisory only):

lenscheck init            # writes .github/workflows/lenscheck.yml (comments, never blocks)
git add .github/workflows/lenscheck.yml && git commit -m "add lenscheck" && git push

Prefer to click around? lenscheck serve opens a local web UI with the flow graph.

That's the whole tool: a flow graph of what a PR does, and rules it can enforce. Everything
below is depth for when you want it.

📌1. What is Lenscheck (in one minute)

When you open a Pull Request (PR), the reviewer sees a diff — red lines removed, green lines
added. But a diff tells you what text changed, not what it means. Did this PR add a new way
into your app? Did it start writing to your database without a login check? Did someone's email
address just start leaving your server?

Lenscheck reads your PR and tells you what it *means* — in a few high-signal findings, each pointing
at the exact line to look at. It's built for Python web apps (Django / Django REST Framework today).

It is not an AI that guesses. It reads your code with Python's own parser and reports facts.
When it isn't sure, it says so (you'll see a ⚠). It never dresses up "I didn't see it" as "it's safe."

📌2. Two features, two problems

Lenscheck has a lot of features, but they exist to serve two that matter most. If you remember
nothing else from this guide, remember these two.

🔽1) See what a PR means — not just what changed

The problem. A git diff shows you text — hundreds of red and green lines. It doesn't tell you
that one of them opened a new endpoint, started writing to the database, or sent a user's email out
of the building. On a big (often AI-generated) PR, the reviewer skims — and the risky change ships.

What Lenscheck does. It reads the code before and after the PR and turns the diff into
meaning: what changed → how it flows → where to look. A huge diff becomes a short, ranked list
plus a flow graph of each change (route → auth → DB tables → external → cache → async → PII). On a
real 17,841-line PR, that came out to 3 things to look at.

Git tells you what lines changed. Lenscheck tells you what those changes mean.

🔽2) Enforce the rules your code already follows — invariants

The problem. Every codebase has rules everyone "knows" — auth before any DB write, personal
data never leaves without a login — but nothing actually enforces them. A PR quietly breaks one, and
it ships.

What Lenscheck does. It discovers those rules from your git history, lets you confirm the
real ones, then enforces them on every PR — flagging (and optionally blocking) a new violation
while ignoring existing debt. This is the part that compounds: over time Lenscheck learns the rules
your codebase cares about, and no competitor has that knowledge.

Everything else is in service of these two. Intent-vs-behaviour contradictions, traced PII leaks,
dependency-capability scanning, SARIF, inline comments, labels, the org roll-up — all of it makes the
two features above sharper. The rest of this guide explains each one, but if the list ever feels like
a lot: it's a flow graph and enforced rules. That's the product.

📌3. Install 

pip install lenscheck-semantic-reviewer

That's it — Lenscheck has zero dependencies (it only uses Python's standard library). You now have a
lenscheck command. Check it:

lenscheck --help

Lenscheck Semantic Reviewer

Usage: lenscheck <command> [options]

Commands:
  init       Add the GitHub Action to this repo (one-command setup)
  review     Run a semantic review of a PR or commit range
  post       Post a review to a PR (sticky comment, inline comments, label)
  serve      Start the Lenscheck web UI
  invariants Discover baseline invariants from a repository's history
  digest     Org-wide roll-up from the labels Lenscheck applies to PRs

📌4. Three ways to use Lenscheck

You can use Lenscheck in whichever way fits:

  1. Web UI — run lenscheck serve, open your browser, click around. Best for exploring and for people who don't live in the terminal. → jump to the tour
  2. Command line — lenscheck review …. Best for scripts, quick checks, and CI. → jump to the CLI
  3. GitHub Action — Lenscheck runs automatically on every PR and comments on it. Best for teams. → jump to the Action

They all share the same engine, so they find the same things.

📌5. The Web UI, panel by panel

Start it inside any repo:

lenscheck serve

It prints a URL (like http://127.0.0.1:8765/) and opens your browser. If you run it inside a git
repo, it auto-detects that repo for you.

The top bar — choosing what to review

Along the top you pick what to compare. You have four ways:

  • PR — pick a merged Pull Request from the dropdown and hit Review.
  • branches — compare two branches (e.g. main → my-feature).
  • commits — compare two commits.
  • Branch vs default button — the one-click shortcut: review your current branch against the main branch. (This is the zero-arg default.)

Reading a review (top to bottom)

Once a review runs, you read it top-to-bottom. Using the screenshot above:

  1. The one-line summary — "This PR adds 1 endpoint, 1 new DB write to AuditLog, 1 new
    external call… and 4 new PII signals."     A plain-English sentence of everything that changed,
    built from facts. (the intent summary)

  2. 🎭 Intent vs. behavior — the red panel. The PR called itself a "refactor / no behavior
    change,"     but Lenscheck found it added an endpoint and started logging an email. When the
    promise and the facts disagree, this panel calls it out. (intent vs. behavior)

  3. 📦 Dependency capability changes — bumped libraries and whether the new version can do more
    than the old one. (dependency scanning)

  4. The tally — 🔴 1 — how many findings at each severity.

  5. The change list (left) — one row per changed endpoint, worst first. Click a row to see…

  6. The flow graph (right) — a live picture of what that endpoint does. In the screenshot,
    ExportUsers → reads User (SQL table auth_user), writes AuditLog (audit_log), calls
    hooks.example.com, reads and writes the cache, and dispatches two async jobs
    (reindex_users, a thread) — every edge colored by kind, with the new parts highlighted. This is
    the same picture Lenscheck can also draw as a
    Mermaid diagram inside a GitHub comment.

  7. The "Where to look" tab — switch the detail pane from the graph to a flat, ranked list of
    every fact with its exact file:line — the WHERE of the review, including the traced leak.

Click any block in the graph (or a line here) and Lenscheck shows you the source, with the exact
line highlighted:

The Invariants panel — teach Lenscheck your rules

Click ⚖ Invariants in the top bar:

Lenscheck samples your git history and shows candidate rules it noticed your codebase following. In
the screenshot:

  • "External/PII egress limited to 2 known destinations" [boundary] — holds 2/2 (100%). It's the rule that makes the ExportUsers change dangerous: the new endpoint would send an email to a third destination, widening that boundary.
  • Each rule has a Confirm button (freeze it as a rule Lenscheck will enforce from now on); rules with exceptions also get a 🩸 Blame button (find the commit that first broke it).

This is the moat — over time you teach Lenscheck the rules your codebase cares about, and no
competitor has that knowledge. (invariants)

Note: the Confirm buttons only appear if you started the server with a place to save them:
lenscheck serve --invariants my-rules.json. Without that, the panel is read-only (Lenscheck never writes
a file you didn't ask for).

Handy web tricks

  • http://…/?open=0 — deep-link that opens the review with the first change already selected.
  • http://…/?invariants=1 — deep-link that opens the Invariants panel automatically.

📌6. The CLI, command by command

lenscheck init — one-command setup

Drops a ready-to-run GitHub Action into the current repo — the fastest way to adopt.

lenscheck init            # writes .github/workflows/lenscheck.yml in advisory mode (comments, never blocks)
lenscheck init --gate     # start it blocking on a confirmed-rule violation instead
lenscheck init --force    # overwrite an existing workflow

It refuses to clobber an existing workflow unless you pass --force, and prints the two remaining
steps (commit, open a PR). Start advisory; switch to --gate once your rules are confirmed and trusted.

lenscheck review — the main event

Analyze a PR / branch / commit and print a review.

The same review as a self-contained HTML file (--html) you can send to anyone — no install
needed:


lenscheck review                       # no args: review THIS branch vs the default branch
lenscheck review /path/to/repo --base main --head my-feature
lenscheck review https://github.com/owner/repo --pr 123

Positional argument:

Argument Meaning
repo A local folder or a GitHub URL. Optional — leave it out and Lenscheck uses the repo you're standing in.

Flags — how to pick what to compare (choose one; or none to auto-detect):

Flag What it does
(nothing) Review the current branch vs. the default branch. The zero-effort mode.
--pr 123 Review a real GitHub Pull Request by number (needs a GitHub URL as the repo).
--base X --head Y Review the difference between two refs (branches, tags, or commit SHAs).
--commit SHA Review a single commit (compares it against its parent).
--merge SHA Review a merge commit (compares its two parents).

Flags — what to produce:

Flag What it does
--out FILE Where to write the Markdown report. Default: pr_review.md.
--json FILE Also write the full review as structured JSON (for tools/automation).
--html FILE Also write a self-contained HTML viewer you can open in a browser.
--sarif FILE Also write SARIF — the format GitHub reads to show findings in its Security tab. (SARIF output)
--invariants FILE Enforce a confirmed rules file: flag any endpoint in this PR that breaks a rule.
--fail-on violation Exit with an error if the PR breaks a confirmed rule. (Use in CI to block merges.)
--fail-on crit Exit with an error on any 🔴 finding.

lenscheck post — put the review on the PR

Takes a review you already generated and posts it to a GitHub PR.

lenscheck post 123 pr_review.md --json pr_review.json --inline --label
Argument / flag What it does
123 The PR number.
pr_review.md The Markdown body to post as a sticky comment (it updates in place on re-runs).
--json FILE The structured review (needed for --inline and --label).
--inline Post each finding as a comment pinned to the exact changed line. (inline comments)
--label Put one lenscheck:* label on the PR based on its worst finding. (auto-label)
--dry-run Print what would be posted, without touching GitHub. Great for testing.

(Needs a GITHUB_TOKEN env var and the gh CLI, which GitHub's runners already have.)

lenscheck serve — the web UI 

lenscheck serve --repo /path/to/repo --port 8765
Flag What it does
--repo Repo to preload (default: the git repo of the current folder).
--invariants FILE The rules file to enforce and the file the Confirm buttons write to.
--port / --host Where to serve (default 8765 on 0.0.0.0).
--pr / --commit / --merge / --base / --head Open straight into a specific review on load.
--no-open Don't auto-open a browser window.

Useful environment variables for a hosted deployment:

Env var What it does
PORT / HOST Where to bind (hosts like Render set PORT; default HOST is 0.0.0.0).
LENSCHECK_TOKEN Require ?token=… on API calls — set this on any public deployment.
LENSCHECK_ALLOWED_REPOS Comma-separated allow-list; only matching repos may be reviewed.
LENSCHECK_BASE_PATH Serve under a sub-path (e.g. /lenscheck) behind a reverse proxy.
LENSCHECK_DEFAULT_REPO The repo shown by default in the UI.
LENSCHECK_INVARIANTS Default invariant corpus path to enforce in the UI.
LENSCHECK_CACHE Where cloned repos are cached (default ~/.cache/lenscheck/repos).
LENSCHECK_GIT_TIMEOUT Seconds before a git clone/archive is aborted (guards huge repos).
GITHUB_TOKEN For private repos / to avoid GitHub rate limits.

To host one shared Lenscheck UI: run lenscheck serve --no-open behind your usual reverse proxy, set
LENSCHECK_TOKEN (so the API isn't open), and optionally LENSCHECK_ALLOWED_REPOS to fence it to just your
repos. To run Lenscheck across all your repos from one place, see
§9 — Set up Lenscheck for all your repos.

lenscheck invariants — discover, confirm, and blame rules

Three jobs in one command.

Discover — look through git history and propose candidate rules:

lenscheck invariants /path/to/repo --snapshots 8
Flag What it does
--snapshots N How many points in history to sample (more = slower but more confident).
--out FILE Where to write the discovered candidates (JSON).
--report FILE Where to write a human-readable report (Markdown).

Confirm — turn candidates into a rules file without hand-editing JSON:

lenscheck invariants --confirm                       # interactive: press c / f / s / q per rule
lenscheck invariants --confirm --id auth-before-write --owner security   # scripted
Flag What it does
--confirm Enter confirm mode. Interactive unless you pass --id or --all.
--in FILE The discovered candidates to read from.
--corpus FILE The confirmed rules file to create/update.
--id NAME Confirm a specific rule (repeatable).
--all Confirm every candidate.
--owner NAME Record who owns the rule.
--drop-baseline Treat today's exceptions as bugs to fix, not as accepted.

In interactive mode you press one key per rule: confirm · fix (confirm, but the current
exceptions are bugs) · skip · quit.

Blame — find the commit that first broke a rule (semantic blame):

lenscheck invariants /path/to/repo --blame auth-before-write --exact
Flag What it does
--blame NAME Which rule to investigate.
--route R Only blame a specific endpoint.
--exact Pinpoint the precise commit (binary-searches history; a bit slower). Without it, you get the window between two sampled snapshots.

lenscheck digest — the org-wide roll-up for leadership

Every other command answers "is **this* PR risky?". digest answers the question a manager
actually asks: *"across **all* our repos, how much risk is sitting in review right now?"* — in one
short message, with no re-analysis and no GitHub Advanced Security.

It works by counting labels. Each PR review applies exactly one lenscheck:* triage label
(auto-label); the digest just searches an org for the open PRs still
carrying each one:

lenscheck digest --org my-org --slack "$SLACK_WEBHOOK"

*Lenscheck digest — my-org*  (open PRs by risk)
🔴  4  security / PII / unauth write
🟠  9  money path
🟡 12  new DB write / external

With --slack, that lands in your channel every morning — one number the whole team (and leadership)
can read without opening a single PR:

Flag What it does
--org ORG The GitHub org/owner to summarize (required).
--repos FILE Optional file of owner/repo lines → adds an adoption line: how many repos have the workflow live and a confirmed invariants file.
--slack URL Post the digest to a Slack incoming webhook (otherwise it just prints).

Needs a GITHUB_TOKEN with org read access (the default per-repo token can't search the org).
An honesty rule carries over from the analyzer: a tier it couldn't fetch shows ?, never a
fake 0. Run it on a schedule (a weekly cron in a central repo) and it becomes the standing
answer to "is Lenscheck worth keeping on?" — because the labels feed it, keep label: true and
issues: write on your review workflow.

📌7. Every feature explained

Each heading below is the problem the feature solves. The first two are the headline features from
§2; everything after them is supporting cast that sharpens those two.
Skim to what's relevant — you don't need to read all eleven.

A diff shows text, not meaning

The semantic diff, severity & flow graph — headline feature ①. Lenscheck analyzes your code
before and after the PR and reports the change in behavior. Renaming a function with no
behavior change? Silence (that's a good thing). Adding an unauthenticated database write? 🔴. Every
finding is ranked 🔴/🟠/🟡/🟢, points at a file:line, and gets a flow graph of what the endpoint
does (route → auth → DB tables → external → cache → async → PII).

Your codebase rules are not enforced

Invariants: discover, confirm, enforce, blame — headline feature ②. The compounding asset. Four steps:

  1. Discover (lenscheck invariants) — mine history for rules your code already follows: 
   ⚠ NEAR-MISS — Authenticated access before any DB write
   - holds: 3/4 endpoints (75%)  ·  persistence: 100% → 100% → 100% → 75% across 4 snapshots
   - exceptions — look here (1):
       - api/users/export — open (AllowAny)  (shop/views.py:40)

  1. Confirm (lenscheck invariants --confirm, or the web button) — mark the ones that are real. Saved
    to a rules file. No JSON editing.

  2. Enforce (lenscheck review --invariants rules.json) — every future PR that breaks a confirmed
    rule gets a 🔴, and --fail-on violation can block the merge.

  3. Blame (lenscheck invariants --blame … --exact) — find exactly which commit broke a rule:

   🩸 auth-before-write first broke at e23c96a (exact, in window 3e9817b..e23c96a)
      holds 3/4 at the snapshot.
      offending endpoint(s):
        - api/users/export — open (AllowAny) (shop/views.py:40)

Bootstrap (turn it on everywhere, no human): confirming rules per repo doesn't scale to 20
repos. lenscheck invariants <repo> --bootstrap --baseline org-baseline.json discovers the rules,
auto-confirms the safe ones, and freezes today's state as the baseline — so the rule file is a
ratchet: it only fires on a new violation a PR introduces, never on existing debt. Seed it
with a shared org baseline (the universal rules) and every repo inherits the same policy; each
repo's own exceptions are filled in automatically. Auto-confirmed rules are tagged
owner: auto-bootstrap so a human can review them later. This is what makes the moat adoptable
across a whole org instead of one repo at a time.

Everything below supports the two above.

You still have to read the whole PR

The intent summary. One plain-English sentence at the top of every review, built from verified facts:

"This PR adds 1 endpoint, 1 new DB write to AuditLog, 1 new external call to
hooks.example.com/export and 4 new PII signals."

Other tools generate this with an AI that reads the diff and sometimes makes things up. Lenscheck counts
real facts, so every number traces to a line.

The PR description contradicts the code

Intent vs. behavior. Your PR title/description is a promise. Lenscheck checks it against the facts.

  • Says "refactor / no behavior change" but added an endpoint or a DB write → 🔴 "claims refactor, but behavior changed here."
  • Says "docs only" but code changed → flagged.

From the demo, the PR titled "refactor: tidy up user views" got caught twice:

🎭 Intent vs. behavior — PR describes itself as "refactor / no behavior change", but the facts disagree
🔴 claims refactor / no behavior change, but adds an endpoint — api/users/export @ shop/views.py:40
🔴 claims refactor / no behavior change, but new PII signal: email → log.info — api/profile @ shop/views.py:32

Is it a real leak, or a coincidence?

PII taint — the precision feature. Old tools say "personal data and an external call are both in
this function — maybe it leaks." Vague. Lenscheck follows the data:

  • If an email actually flows into an external call / log / response → ✅ verified: email → requests.post @ line 46. The exact field, the exact exit, the exact line.
  • If they just co-exist with no traced path → it stays ⚠ potential (honest, no false alarm).
  • If the data passes through a function Lenscheck doesn't recognize (which might clean it) → it refuses to call it a confirmed leak.

It also resolves fuzzy database writes: for order in Order.objects.filter(...): order.save() is now
understood as writing the Order table, not a vague <instance>.

A dependency bump quietly gains new powers

Dependency capability-delta. When a PR bumps a library, Lenscheck downloads the old and new
versions and compares what each can do — checking for network / subprocess / native code / file
writes / reading secrets. It reports only the newly gained powers:

  • requests 2.28→2.31: no new capabilities 🟢
  • leftpad 1.0→2.0: now spawns a subprocess 🔴

If it can't fetch a version (offline, or the package has no source), it says ⚠ unresolved — never
"safe":

📦 Dependency capability changes
⚠ requests 2.28.0→2.31.0 — capabilities not statically resolved (offline or no sdist)
⚠ six 1.15.0→1.16.0 — capabilities not statically resolved (offline or no sdist)

Turn the network scan off with LENSCHECK_SCAN_DEPS=0 (or the Action's scan_deps: false) and you'll
always get the fast ⚠ mode.

A text list does not show the flow

Mermaid flow diagram. Every review's Markdown includes a Mermaid sequence diagram of the
before→after flow. GitHub renders it right inside the PR comment — a real picture of your endpoint's
behavior, drawn from facts, not by an AI:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant NExportUsers as ExportUsers
    Client->>NExportUsers: 🆕 POST api/users/export
    NExportUsers->>Database: write AuditLog
    NExportUsers->>Database: read User
    NExportUsers->>External: https://hooks.example.com/export
```

GitHub renders that right inside the PR comment — a real picture of the endpoint's behavior, drawn
from facts:

The finding is not next to the code

Inline PR comments. lenscheck post … --inline pins each finding as a comment on the exact
line. The honest guard: it only pins a comment where it can prove the line is in the diff (GitHub
rejects anything else); the rest roll into the one sticky summary comment.

A queue of PRs is hard to triage

Auto-label. lenscheck post … --label puts one triage label on the PR based on its worst
finding: lenscheck:🔴security / lenscheck:🟠payment / lenscheck:🟡new-write /
lenscheck:🟢safe-refactor. Makes a queue of PRs scannable at a glance.

Findings belong in the Security tab

SARIF output. --sarif pr_review.sarif writes a standard file GitHub understands. Upload it and
your findings show up on the exact changed lines in the PR's "Files changed" tab and in the repo's
Security tab — native, official, high-visibility.

A review should not need arguments

Smart default target. Running lenscheck review with no arguments inside a repo just does the
obvious thing: reviews your current branch vs. the default branch. If you're on the default
branch, it tells you to switch to a feature branch instead of guessing.

📌8. The GitHub Action, input by input

Add this workflow and Lenscheck reviews every PR automatically:

# .github/workflows/lenscheck.yml
name: Lenscheck Semantic Review
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write     # to post comments
  issues: write            # to apply the label
  security-events: write   # to upload SARIF
jobs:
  lenscheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: AnkushSinghGandhi/lenscheck-semantic-reviewer@v1
        with:
          fail_on: none          # or: violation | crit

Every input:

Input Default What it does
github_token auto Token for reading the PR and posting back.
fail_on none violation fails the build on a broken rule; crit fails on any 🔴.
invariants (none) Path to a confirmed rules file to enforce.
comment true Post the sticky summary comment.
inline true Also post inline comments on changed lines. (inline)
label true Apply one lenscheck:* label. (label)
scan_deps true Scan bumped dependencies against PyPI. Set false to skip the network (findings become ⚠). (deps)
upload_sarif true Upload SARIF to code scanning. Set false on private repos without GitHub Advanced Security so the step is skipped and the check stays green.

The Action uploads SARIF (when upload_sarif is on), so findings appear in the Security tab —
that surface needs GitHub Advanced Security on private repos. Without GHAS, the same findings still
arrive as the PR comment, inline comments, and label, and an org-wide roll-up is available via
lenscheck digest (below).

📌9. Set up Lenscheck for all your repos

Section 8 put Lenscheck on one repo. This section turns it on across every repo you own —
personal projects, a team's services, or a whole company — from one place, with almost no
per-repo work.

The trick: host the workflow once, and have every repo point at it. Then you switch Lenscheck on (or
change how it behaves) by editing a single file, not twenty. It's the same steps whether you have 1
repo or 100.

Step 1 — Put the workflow in one central repo

Make a repo — call it lenscheck-workflows (under your username or org) — and add the real workflow
there once, as a reusable workflow:

# lenscheck-workflows/.github/workflows/lenscheck.yml
name: Lenscheck
on: { workflow_call: {} }
permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write, issues: write }
jobs:
  lenscheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: AnkushSinghGandhi/lenscheck-semantic-reviewer@v1
        with:
          comment: 'true'
          fail_on: none          # observe mode — never blocks a merge (yet)
          upload_sarif: false    # set true only if you have GitHub Advanced Security

Then every repo gets a tiny 3-line caller that just points at it:

# any-repo/.github/workflows/lenscheck.yml
name: Lenscheck
on: { pull_request: {} }
jobs:
  lenscheck:
    uses: your-name/lenscheck-workflows/.github/workflows/lenscheck.yml@v1
    permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write, issues: write }

Now updating Lenscheck everywhere means editing one file in lenscheck-workflows. That's the
"centralised" part — and it's identical for a personal account, a team, or an org.

Step 2 — Start in "observe mode" (comment, never block)

Notice fail_on: none above. That's observe mode: Lenscheck posts its review on every PR but
can never block a merge. Zero risk — you and your team see the value for a week or two before it
can ever get in the way. You turn on blocking later, once you trust it (Step 5).

Keep issues: write + label: 'true' on. Lenscheck puts one lenscheck:* label on each PR, and Step 4's
roll-up counts those labels — no label, no roll-up.

Adding the caller to many repos: for a handful, paste it in by hand. For a lot, a small script
that loops your repo list and opens the 3-line PR on each (using the gh CLI) does it in one go — or,
on GitHub Enterprise, an org "required workflow" applies it automatically.

Step 3 — Turn on your rules (the moat), everywhere, automatically

This is the part that makes Lenscheck yours: enforcing the promises your code already keeps
("always log in before writing to the DB", "personal data never leaves without auth"). Normally you'd
discover rules, confirm each by hand, and commit a file — fine for one repo, tedious for many.

lenscheck invariants --bootstrap does it with no human:

lenscheck invariants <repo> --bootstrap --baseline org-baseline.json --out lenscheck-invariants.json

It finds the repo's rules, auto-confirms the safe ones, and freezes today's state as the starting
line — so it only ever complains about a new violation a future PR introduces, never your existing
code. Zero noise.

Write your shared rules once in an org-baseline.json (start from
org-baseline.sample.json) — the universal ones like auth before any
DB write and no new external destination for personal data — and every repo inherits them. Commit
each repo's lenscheck-invariants.json, and the workflow enforces it from then on.

Step 4 — Get one number across all your repos (optional)

Per-PR comments help whoever's on that PR. For the big picture — how many risky PRs are open
right now — lenscheck digest counts the open PRs carrying each lenscheck:* label:

lenscheck digest --org your-github-org --slack "$SLACK_WEBHOOK"

🔴  4  security / PII / unauth write
🟠  9  money path
🟡 12  new DB write / external

No re-analysis, and no GitHub Advanced Security needed — it just reads the labels. Run it on a
weekly schedule and pipe it to Slack. (This one aggregates a whole GitHub org; for personal repos
the per-PR labels already give you the same signal on each PR.)

Step 5 — Start blocking merges — last, and only on the sure things

Once people trust the reviews, flip the switch in your one central file — and only for the
highest-confidence signal:

      - uses: AnkushSinghGandhi/lenscheck-semantic-reviewer@v1
        with:
          fail_on: violation     # block only when a PR breaks a confirmed rule

Never block on "any 🔴" from day one — that's how a tool gets switched off. Block only on a new rule
violation, once your rules are confirmed and trusted.

One security note before you go wide

If other people will depend on this, mirror the Action into your own account/org and pin a commit
SHA instead of pointing at a public @v1 tag — the reusable workflow means you fix that in one
place. And to reassure any security reviewer: Lenscheck never runs your code — it reads it with
Python's parser and analyzes clean git snapshots, so there's nothing to execute.

📌10. A full worked example

Here's the exact scenario from the screenshots. A developer opens a PR titled
"refactor: tidy up user views." It claims to be a harmless cleanup. In reality it:

  • adds POST /api/users/export with no login required (AllowAny),
  • inside it, writes to the AuditLog table and sends a user's email to an external webhook,
  • and changes GET /api/profile to log the user's email,
  • while bumping requests and six.

Run it:

lenscheck review /path/to/repo --commit <sha> --sarif out.sarif

Lenscheck produces, in one pass:

  • Summary: "adds 1 endpoint, 1 new DB write to AuditLog, 1 new external call… and 4 new PII signals."
  • 🎭 Contradiction: "claims refactor, but adds an endpoint" and "…but new PII signal: email → log.info."
  • 🔴 NEW ENDPOINT api/users/export: "new endpoint exposes a PII path with open/unspecified auth" — with the verified leak email → requests.post @ shop/views.py:46.
  • 📦 Dependencies: the two bumps (with capabilities, or ⚠ offline).
  • 🔀 Flow diagram: the Mermaid picture above.

Every single item points to a line you can click. Nothing was guessed.

📌11. Honesty rules

Lenscheck's whole value is that you can trust it. So it follows strict rules:

  • Never render "not observed" as "doesn't exist." If Lenscheck can't follow something, it shows ⚠ or ? — never a false all-clear.
  • A "verified" finding is really verified. The PII taint only says ✅ when it saw the whole path; if data might have been sanitized, it stays ⚠.
  • No arbitrary file writes, no surprise network. The web "Confirm" only writes the file you configured; dependency scanning can be turned off.
  • Every number traces to a file:line. Because Lenscheck reports facts, not vibes.

📌12. Quick reference card 

# review
lenscheck review                                  # this branch vs default branch
lenscheck review . --base main --head feature     # two refs
lenscheck review URL --pr 123                      # a GitHub PR
lenscheck review . --commit <sha>                  # one commit
lenscheck review . --sarif out.sarif --html r.html # extra outputs
lenscheck review . --invariants rules.json --fail-on violation   # enforce + block

# post to a PR
lenscheck post 123 pr_review.md --json pr_review.json --inline --label
lenscheck post 123 pr_review.md --dry-run          # preview, no posting

# web UI
lenscheck serve                                    # this repo
lenscheck serve --repo . --invariants rules.json   # + enable Confirm buttons

# invariants (rules)
lenscheck invariants .                             # discover candidate rules
lenscheck invariants --confirm                     # confirm interactively
lenscheck invariants --confirm --id auth-before-write --owner security
lenscheck invariants . --bootstrap --baseline org-baseline.json   # auto-confirm + ratchet (no human)
lenscheck invariants . --blame auth-before-write --exact   # who broke it

# digest (org-wide roll-up for leadership)
lenscheck digest --org my-org                       # open PRs by lenscheck:* label
lenscheck digest --org my-org --repos repos.txt --slack "$SLACK_WEBHOOK"  # + adoption, to Slack

# env vars
LENSCHECK_SCAN_DEPS=0     # skip the dependency network scan
LENSCHECK_TOKEN=…         # lock down a hosted `lenscheck serve`
LENSCHECK_CACHE=…         # where cloned repos are cached (default ~/.cache/lenscheck/repos)
LENSCHECK_GIT_TIMEOUT=…   # seconds before a git clone/archive is aborted

📌Glossary (words you need to know)

You'll meet these terms everywhere. Here they are in plain English.

Endpoint — a single "door" into your web app. A URL + the code that runs when someone hits it.
Example: POST /api/users/export runs the ExportUsers function. Lenscheck reviews your PR one
endpoint at a time.

The 7-edge lens — for each endpoint, Lenscheck asks seven simple questions (these are the "edges"):

Edge The question it answers
Route What URL is this, and which function handles it?
Auth Do you need to be logged in? (or is it open to anyone?)
DB Does it read or write the database? Which tables?
External Does it call the outside world? (Stripe, a webhook, an API…)
Async Does it kick off a background job? (Celery, a thread…)
Cache Does it read or invalidate the cache? Which keys?
PII Does it touch personal data (email, phone, address…)?

Severity colors — Lenscheck ranks every finding by how much it should worry you:

  • 🔴 critical — security / data-flow (e.g. an open endpoint writing to the DB)
  • 🟠 high — money paths (payments, orders)
  • 🟡 medium — a new write or a dependency change
  • 🟢 low — a safe refactor, nothing risky

PII — "Personally Identifiable Information": personal data like an email, phone number,
address, password, card number. Leaking it is a legal and trust problem.

PII egress — "egress" just means leaving. PII egress = personal data leaving your
server — sent to an external API, written to a log, or returned to the browser. That's the moment
that matters.

Taint — following a piece of data as it moves through the code. If an email is "tainted," Lenscheck
watches whether that exact value reaches an exit (an external call, a log, a response). If it
does, that's a confirmed leak.

Invariant — a rule your codebase has always followed, whether or not anyone wrote it down.
Example: "every endpoint that writes to the database first checks you're logged in." Lenscheck can
discover these from your git history, let you confirm the real ones, and then enforce
them on every PR.

Semantic diff — a normal diff compares text. A semantic diff compares meaning: Lenscheck
analyzes your code before and after the PR and reports the difference in behavior (new
endpoints, new DB writes, new calls…), ignoring cosmetic changes like renaming a function.

📌Companion tool: lenscheck-contract

Everything above happens before merge — the reviewer discovers the rules your code follows and
flags a PR that breaks one. Its companion, lenscheck-contract
(a tiny, MIT-licensed runtime library), closes the loop at runtime: your app keeps a declared list
of what each endpoint is allowed to do — write these tables, call these hosts — and can't lie about
it. An undeclared DB write or a new external call is blocked (or logged) the moment it happens.

So a rule you confirmed here — "auth before any DB write," "personal data never leaves without
auth" — can be declared once and enforced in production, not just checked in review. Same
promise, two moments: the reviewer catches it in the PR; the contract stops it in prod. →
Read the contract guide.

Lenscheck is source-available (Elastic-2.0). Built by Ankush Singh Gandhi. Questions,
stars, and sponsorships welcome on GitHub.

articles.title: "What If Your CSS Compiler Could Catch Accessibility Bugs Before Production?"
articles.description: Modern frontend development has become increasingly sophisticated.  We have component-driven...
articles.body_html:
Modern frontend development has become increasingly sophisticated.

We have component-driven architectures, server components, powerful build tools, automated testing, design systems, and AI coding assistants.

Yet one problem remains surprisingly common:

We still discover many styling and accessibility problems too late.

A color combination fails contrast requirements. A component introduces duplicated CSS. A dark theme needs additional overrides. An RTL layout breaks because physical spacing properties were used. A styling engine adds work to the browser that could have been completed during the build.

What if your styling system could prevent these problems before your application ships?

That is the idea behind "traceless-style" (https://traceless-style.dev/).

It is an open-source, MIT-licensed, build-time atomic CSS library designed around three principles:

  • Zero-runtime styling for compiled style declarations.
  • Automated accessibility validation.
  • Intelligent styling diagnostics and transformations.

Let's explore what this approach looks like in practice.

  1. Move CSS work from runtime to build time

Traditional runtime CSS-in-JS approaches can involve generating class names, processing styles, maintaining caches, or inserting CSS rules while an application runs.

These operations are not necessarily expensive in every application, but they introduce work that may be avoidable.

traceless-style takes a different approach.

Instead of processing compiled styles in the browser, it transforms "tl.create()" calls during the build process into ordinary class-name strings.

For example:

import { tl } from "traceless-style";

const $ = tl.create({
card: {
padding: "1.5rem",
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_hover: {
  transform: "translateY(-2px)",
},

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

export function Card() {
return (


Build faster. Ship cleaner.

);
}

During compilation, the styling declaration is transformed into generated class names, while the corresponding atomic CSS rules are emitted into a static stylesheet.

The result:

  • No runtime styling engine for transformed declarations.
  • No runtime style injection for compiled styles.
  • Reusable atomic CSS rules.
  • Automatic deduplication of identical property-value combinations.
  • A stylesheet generated before production deployment.

The browser receives the compiled output rather than having to interpret the original styling object.

The central idea is simple: do the styling work before the user visits the application.

Technical explanation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/01-introduction

  1. Accessibility should be part of the build process

This is where the project takes an interesting direction.

Accessibility is often handled through manual reviews, separate testing tools, or checks performed late in development.

But color contrast problems can be introduced by something as simple as changing a text color or background.

traceless-style includes build-time contrast validation based on WCAG requirements.

It checks relevant contrast requirements, including:

  • WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text.
  • WCAG AAA: 7:1 for normal text.
  • UI component contrast requirements.
  • Focus-indicator contrast requirements.

It also provides APCA Lc readings as an additional perception-oriented measurement.

Consider this diagnostic example:

traceless-style build

✘ TLS0301 app/Button.tsx:24:7

WCAG 2.1 §1.4.3
AA 4.5:1 not met.

Foreground: #94a3b8
Background: #ffffff

Contrast ratio: 2.85:1

Suggested replacement: #475569
Contrast ratio: 7.55:1

Run with --fix-contrast to apply.

Instead of discovering the issue after deployment, developers can receive actionable feedback during the build process.

The interactive contrast-fixing workflow can also suggest alternative colors.

This changes the role of accessibility from a final checklist into part of the development workflow.

Important: automated contrast checks do not replace complete accessibility testing, keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, or evaluation with real users.

Documentation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs

  1. Automatic dark mode without duplicating every color

Dark mode is easy to demonstrate and surprisingly easy to implement inconsistently.

A typical application may contain hundreds of components, each with different backgrounds, text colors, borders, and interactive states.

Maintaining all those variations manually can become difficult.

traceless-style can derive dark variants for colors during compilation, while allowing explicit overrides when necessary.

For example:

const $ = tl.create({
panel: {
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

You can retain control over individual dark-mode decisions without manually duplicating every declaration.

The goal is to make theme support part of the styling architecture rather than a separate layer of repetitive CSS.

  1. RTL support built into the styling workflow

Global applications need more than English interfaces.

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and other right-to-left languages introduce additional layout requirements.

Developers frequently encounter problems when using physical CSS properties such as:

margin-left: 16px;
padding-right: 12px;

A layout designed around physical directions can become difficult to maintain across LTR and RTL interfaces.

traceless-style supports automatic RTL transformations by rewriting physical properties into logical CSS equivalents during compilation.

For example, a left-side margin can be transformed into its logical inline-start equivalent.

This is particularly useful for teams building multilingual applications and shared design systems.

One styling architecture can serve different writing directions without requiring developers to maintain separate copies of every component.

  1. Atomic CSS and stylesheet deduplication

Large applications often contain repeated styling declarations across many components.

Atomic CSS addresses this by representing individual CSS property-value combinations as reusable classes.

Imagine hundreds of components using:

display: flex;

Rather than repeatedly emitting identical declarations, the compiler can reuse the corresponding generated atomic rule.

traceless-style also provides:

  • "tl.defineTokens()" for design tokens.
  • "tl.createTheme()" for theme creation.
  • "tl.merge()" for style composition.
  • "tl.cx()" for class composition.
  • "tl.extend()" for reusable style extensions.
  • "tl.keyframes()" for animations.

This creates a more structured styling environment as an application grows.

  1. More than a CSS library: a developer tooling ecosystem

A modern developer tool should fit into the workflow developers already use.

The traceless-style ecosystem includes:

Compiler

Transforms styling declarations into generated atomic CSS during the build.

CLI

Provides commands for initialization, extraction, development, production builds, auditing, and inspection.

VS Code extension

Provides features including autocomplete, color swatches, hover documentation, and inline diagnostics.

Browser DevTools extension

Helps inspect generated styling classes in the browser.

Framework integrations

Supports environments including:

  • Next.js
  • Vite
  • Remix
  • Astro
  • SvelteKit
  • Qwik
  • Solid
  • Webpack
  • Rollup
  • esbuild

The objective is not simply to introduce another way to write CSS.

It is to create a connected workflow covering styling, compilation, validation, and debugging.

  1. Install it and try it in a real project

You can install traceless-style using npm:

npm install traceless-style

Or pnpm:

pnpm add traceless-style

Then initialize your project:

npx traceless-style init

Start the development workflow:

npx traceless-style dev

For production:

npx traceless-style build

You can also run the contrast-fixing workflow:

npx traceless-style --fix-contrast

The initialization command detects supported project frameworks and helps configure the integration.

No complicated setup process is required for the standard supported configurations.

Start with a small component, inspect the generated CSS, and evaluate the workflow in your own project.

  1. Why this approach matters as AI-assisted development grows

AI coding tools are changing how frontend applications are created.

Developers can now generate components, layouts, themes, and entire application interfaces much faster than before.

But generating code is not the same as generating reliable production-ready code.

AI-generated interfaces can still contain:

  • Poor color contrast.
  • Inconsistent design tokens.
  • Duplicated styling declarations.
  • Incorrect RTL behavior.
  • Unnecessary runtime styling work.

A build-time styling system with automated validation offers another layer of engineering discipline.

Instead of relying entirely on developers or AI assistants to remember every styling rule, the compiler can enforce defined constraints.

This is an interesting direction for the future of frontend infrastructure.

  1. Open source and developer contributions

traceless-style is released under the MIT license.

Developers can explore the implementation, evaluate its architecture, use it in their projects, and contribute improvements.

The project is actively documented through its official documentation and source repository.

Useful resources:

  • Official website: https://traceless-style.dev/
  • Documentation: https://traceless-style.dev/docs
  • Installation guide: https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/02-installation
  • npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style
  • VS Code extension: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=SparkGoldenTech.traceless-style-vscode
  1. Let's discuss the future of CSS tooling

I would love to hear from frontend engineers, open-source maintainers, and developers working on large applications.

A few questions:

  1. Do you prefer build-time CSS compilation over runtime CSS-in-JS?
  2. Should accessibility validation be a mandatory part of every production build?
  3. Would automatic dark-mode and RTL transformations simplify your design system?
  4. How should CSS tooling evolve to support AI-generated interfaces?
  5. What would you improve in a zero-runtime styling architecture?

If you are interested in modern CSS architecture, frontend performance, accessibility engineering, or developer tooling, give traceless-style a try.

Install it. Test it against a real component. Inspect the generated output. Share your feedback.

Explore the project:

https://traceless-style.dev/

GitHub:
https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style

npm:
https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style

articles.title: Uploading a 5 GB video just to transcribe it? Extract the audio in the browser first
articles.description: If someone wants a transcript of a 2-hour screen recording, the file on their disk might be 4 GB. But...
articles.body_html:
If someone wants a transcript of a 2-hour screen recording, the file on their disk might be 4 GB. But the part a speech-to-text model needs is the sound, and speech models work at 16 kHz mono anyway. At 32 kbps Opus, an hour of mono speech is about 14 MB. Ten hours is about 144 MB.

So for TranscribeLink I stopped asking people to upload the video. The browser pulls the audio track out first and uploads only that. Here's how it works and what I had to get right.

The tools: WebCodecs + Mediabunny

WebCodecs gives the browser access to native audio encoders and decoders (AudioDecoder, AudioEncoder). On its own it doesn't read containers like MP4, MOV, MKV or WebM. For that I use Mediabunny, a small library that demuxes and muxes those formats in the browser and drives WebCodecs for you.

The core of it is a "conversion" that drops the video track and re-encodes the audio:

const input = new Input({ source: new BlobSource(file), formats: ALL_FORMATS });
if (!(await input.getPrimaryAudioTrack())) throw new Error('No audio track');

const output = new Output({ format: new OggOutputFormat(), target: new BufferTarget() });
const conversion = await Conversion.init({
  input, output,
  video: { discard: true },
  audio: { codec: 'opus', numberOfChannels: 1, sampleRate: 16000, bitrate: 32000, forceTranscode: true },
});
conversion.onProgress = (p) => showProgress(p);
await conversion.execute();

const audio = new File([output.target.buffer], 'audio.ogg', { type: 'audio/ogg' });

BlobSource reads the file in slices, so a 5 GB video never has to fit in memory.

Fallbacks matter more than the happy path

Not every browser can encode Opus. I try two targets in order and check each one first with canEncodeAudio:

  1. Opus, mono, 16 kHz, 32 kbps, in an Ogg file (about 14 MB an hour)
  2. AAC, mono, 44.1 kHz, 48 kbps, in an MP4 file (about 22 MB an hour)

If the browser has no AudioEncoder at all (older Safari), or neither codec works, nothing breaks: it just uploads the original file. Extraction is an optimisation, never a requirement.

Don't wait for extraction: race it

Extracting audio from a long file takes time, and on a fast connection the original might upload before extraction finishes. So both start at once:

  • The original file starts uploading in chunks right away.
  • Extraction runs in parallel.
  • When extraction finishes, compare: if the bytes still left to upload are more than the size of the extracted audio, stop the upload, tell the server to replace it, and send the audio instead. Otherwise cancel extraction and let the original finish. 
const first = await Promise.race([
  sending.then((result) => ({ sent: result })),
  extraction.promise.then((audio) => ({ audio }), (error) => ({ audio: null, error })),
]);

if (first.audio && file.size * (1 - uploadedFraction) > first.audio.size) {
  stopUpload();
  await replaceOnServer(first.audio.size);
  await upload(first.audio);
}

On a slow connection the audio almost always wins, and that's exactly where it saves the most time.

Small details that caught me

  • Resumed uploads keep the original. I resume interrupted uploads by byte offset. Extracted audio isn't byte-identical between runs, so a resumed upload continues with the original file instead of re-extracting.
  • Skip tiny files. Below about 1 MB, extraction isn't worth the overhead, so those go up as they are.
  • Load the library early. Mediabunny is about 690 KB minified. I start loading it when the user opens the file picker, so it's ready by the time they've chosen a file.
  • Use XMLHttpRequest for chunks. fetch doesn't report upload progress, so a big chunk shows 0% until it's done. xhr.upload.onprogress lets the progress bar move smoothly, which matters when people are watching a multi-GB upload.

Result

A long video becomes an audio file of tens of megabytes before it leaves the user's machine. The upload that used to be the slowest step is now usually the shortest, and the server never has to store or process the video.

I use this in TranscribeLink, where you can upload files up to 10 hours or 5 GB, or paste a video link, and get a transcript in 100 languages. If you've done something similar, I'd like to hear how you handled browsers without WebCodecs.

articles.title: I'm a School Teacher in Pakistan. I Built 883 Free Tools in 40 Languages — Here's What I Learned
articles.description: I'm a School Teacher in Pakistan. I Built 883 Free Tools in 40 Languages — Here's What I...
articles.body_html:
I'm a School Teacher in Pakistan. I Built 883 Free Tools in 40 Languages — Here's What I Learned

By day, I teach school in Jaranwala, a small city in Punjab, Pakistan. I also train other teachers in how to use AI in their classrooms. In my remaining hours, I run Loona Automation — a network of 30 tool websites holding 883 free tools, every one of them published in 40 language editions.

No sign-up. No downloads. No servers doing the work. Everything runs in the visitor's own browser, on their own device.

This past weekend I shipped 12 new tools in one go. This post is about how that network is built, why I made three unusual decisions — client-side only, 40 languages, and a strict three-check quality rule — and what those decisions have taught me.

The mission behind it: Bolti Duniya

My mission has a name in Urdu: Bolti Duniya — "a world that speaks." The idea is simple: every book should speak, in every language, for everyone who cannot read.

That mission shapes the engineering. If a tool is meant for everyone, it cannot ask for an account. It cannot demand a fast connection to a distant server. It cannot be in English only. And it cannot cost money, because the people who need free tools the most are the ones least able to pay for them.

So the rules for every Loona tool are fixed:

  • Free, with no premium tier hiding the useful part
  • No sign-up, no login, ever
  • Client-side — the work happens on the visitor's device
  • Fast on a cheap phone, because that's what most of my visitors use
  • In the visitor's language, not just mine

Why everything runs in the browser

Client-side-only is the decision people question most, so let me explain it honestly.

A server costs money every month, for every user, forever. A static page on GitHub Pages costs nothing to serve, whether ten people use it or ten thousand. For a one-person project funded by a teacher's salary, that difference is the whole project.

Privacy is the second reason. When someone converts a photo, checks a resume, or generates a class attendance register on Loona, their file never leaves their device. There is nothing to leak because there is nothing to collect. I don't have to ask visitors to trust me with their documents — the architecture makes the promise for me.

The third reason is speed and reliability. No round trip to a server means the tool works the moment the page loads, and it keeps working on the slow connections common in my part of the world.

The honest trade-off: some things simply can't be done well in a browser, and I don't pretend otherwise. I would rather offer 883 tools that genuinely work on-device than promise server-grade features I can't sustain.

Why 40 languages

When someone searches Google in their own language, they deserve to find a tool in that language too. So every Loona site exists in 40 full editions: 35 languages, plus 5 regional variants such as US and UK English and Brazilian and European Portuguese.

These are real translated editions, not a JavaScript text-swap button. Each edition has its own pages, its own navigation, its own search index. That is slower to build and much harder to maintain — 40 editions means every fix has to be verified 40 times — but a teacher in Istanbul or Jakarta should feel the tool was made for them, because it was.

The 12 tools from this weekend

The newest additions, one per real problem I kept seeing:

  1. HEIC to JPG Converter — iPhone photos that won't open anywhere else
  2. Islamic Baby Names — 1,197 names with meanings, for new parents
  3. ATS Resume Checker — will your resume survive the screening software?
  4. Report Card Maker — for teachers like me, at term's end
  5. Certificate Maker — upgraded to print certificates in bulk from a list of names
  6. Signature Background Remover — a clean signature image from a phone photo
  7. Word of the Day — a 500-word bank, one word daily, for learners
  8. Exam Date Sheet Maker — the timetable every school office builds by hand
  9. Attendance Register Generator — a printable register in minutes
  10. Hashtag Generator — for small sellers marketing their own products
  11. Emoji & Symbols Picker — 1,923 emojis and 393 symbols, searchable, one click to copy
  12. Online Alarm Clock — a full-screen clock that works in any browser tab

Every one of them shipped in all 40 editions, not just English.

The three-check rule (and the bugs it caught)

Here is the lesson I would give anyone building in public: never trust your own "done."

Every Loona release now passes three separate checks:

  1. The maker self-tests — whoever built it tests it themselves, on real data.
  2. An independent checker verifies it live — a different set of eyes loads the actual published pages, counts what a visitor would count, and tries to break it.
  3. A fresh-eyes visitor audit — someone walks through it as a first-time visitor, reading everything as if they'd never seen it.

This weekend alone, the second and third checks caught things the builders had missed: a print layout defect in a new tool that only appeared on paper, published tool counts on the hub that no longer matched reality after the new tools landed, and a broken block in one language edition's sitemap. Each one was small. Each one would have been a real visitor's bad experience. All were fixed before I called the work complete.

The rule costs time. It is worth it. A free tool that fails once doesn't get a second chance from most visitors.

What I'd tell another teacher building on the side

Start with one real problem from your own day. Mine were lesson plans, registers, and date sheets — the paperwork of a school. Solve it completely, for free, in the language of the people who have the problem. Then solve the next one. Eight hundred eighty-three tools sounds like a strategy; honestly, it was just that habit, repeated.

The same packs behind some of these tools also exist as 35 AI skills on Agensi, for people who work through AI agents — but the websites remain the heart of it, because a website asks nothing of the visitor at all.

If any of the 883 tools can save you ten minutes this week, they're all in one place:

loonaautomation.github.io

I'd genuinely like to hear which tool you'd want next — the comments are where most of my roadmap comes from.

— Aurang Zeb Loona
School teacher & AI teacher trainer, Jaranwala, Pakistan
Founder, Loona Automation

articles.title: 🐱 The Great Cat Party on necoz Planet! 🚀Python variable
articles.description: Far away in the galaxy, there was a beautiful planet called necoz. 🌌  One day, the King of necoz...
articles.body_html:
Far away in the galaxy, there was a beautiful planet called necoz. 🌌

One day, the King of necoz announced something very exciting:

📢 Attention, everyone! Today we are hosting the biggest Cat Party in the entire galaxy! All cats are invited!

Cats from different galaxies started arriving. Some came by UFO, some came by spaceship, and one cat even arrived on a flying pizza! 🍕

🛸 Scene 1: 30 Cats and a Confused King

The party finally started.

The King looked around and shouted:

WHAT?! There are 30 cats here! Who is going to count all of them?

Suddenly, a little cat wearing sunglasses said:

Bro, just use Python!

The King opened his laptop and wrote:

cats = 30

print(cats)

Output:

30

The King: "WOW! Python counted them without even asking for their names!"

And that's how the King discovered Variables.

A variable is like a container that stores information.

In this example:

  • cats is the variable name.
  • 30 is the value.
  • = is the assignment operator.

🍕 Scene 2: 10 More Hungry Cats!

Suddenly, a UFO landed near the party.

10 more cats came out.

Their leader shouted:

WE WANT FOOD! WE ARE STARVING!

The King replied:

Bro, this is a party, not a free restaurant!

He updated his Python code:

cats = 30

cats = 40

print(cats)

Output:

40

The King: "WAIT! We had 30 cats, and now we have 40!"

That's the magic of variables. We can change the value stored in a variable.

🎂 Scene 3: The Great Cake Disaster

The King ordered 5 cakes for the party.

But one cat grabbed a cake and shouted:

THIS CAKE IS MINE!

Another cat replied:
NO! I SAW IT FIRST!

Meanwhile, a third cat(@hanzla ) was already escaping with the entire cake box. 😂

The King decided to store the information in separate variables.

cats = 40
cakes = 5

print(cats)
print(cakes)

Output:

40
5

Now Python knows that there are 40 cats and 5 cakes.

Each variable stores its own value.

😹 Scene 4: Different Types of Data

The King wanted to record more information about the party.

So he wrote:

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
party_started = True
cake_price = 250.50

His assistant cat asked:

Why do these values look different?

The King explained:

Variable Value Data Type
planet "necoz" String
cats 40 Integer
party_started True Boolean
