cake_price 250.50 Float

Let's understand them:

  • String: Stores text or words.
  • Integer: Stores whole numbers.
  • Boolean: Stores True or False.
  • Float: Stores decimal numbers.

The cat replied:

OMG! So I can also become a variable?

The King: "Yes, but please stop eating the cake!" 😂

💻 Scene 5: The Final Python Experiment

The King decided to display all the party information together.

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
cakes = 5
party_started = True

print("Welcome to", planet)
print("Total Cats:", cats)
print("Total Cakes:", cakes)
print("Party Started:", party_started)

Output:

Welcome to necoz
Total Cats: 40
Total Cakes: 5
Party Started: True

The King shouted:

FINALLY! I AM A PYTHON DEVELOPER!

But suddenly, a cat @effessdev interrupted:
Developer later, bro. First, order 40 more cakes!

And that's how the biggest cat party in the galaxy continued all night. 🐱🎉

articles.title: Stratagem #34: Derek Gave Up Acceptance Sign-Off. The AI Still Can't Tell Who Won.
articles.description: People do not injure themselves without cause; the wound must be real. Mix truth with falsehood, and...
articles.body_html:
People do not injure themselves without cause; the wound must be real. Mix truth with falsehood, and the deception can succeed.

The Thirty-Six Stratagems, Inflicting Injury on Oneself

Previously on this series:

#15: Derek and Alex Shared One Server. Derek discovered that ACL's collector was mirroring diagnostic results, supply-chain orders, and patient-management metadata in full. He worked with Alex to redirect its output. The diagnostic results took a separate route back into the internal pipeline.

#27: Alex Watched the AI Wait. The 800 ms experiment ended. During that call, Alex confirmed that his observation probe was still running.

#33: Mark Reviewed an AI Method. The Reviewer Brought Back a Different Question. The technical conclusion was retained within defined limits. Its supporting sources still needed verification. Mark had not yet sent his request for permission.

Two Names

The lunch bag rested against the monitor stand, still sealed. Derek dragged the schedule across the screen and stopped the cursor over an empty slot. The page header read MediSys's AI-Assisted Diagnostic Validation Platform. His name was in the Quality Validation Lead field.

A new email notification covered one corner of the schedule. The Project Management Office (PMO) had sent a maintenance brief and responsibility matrix for an old hospital integration project. The work package was COL-OUT-04. He was to confirm the external delivery arrangements that afternoon.

Execution owner: Derek Shaw. Acceptance signatory: Derek Shaw. Beneath the names, a note said that closing the package under the normal process required the signatory to confirm the validation results and any outstanding items. The existing authorization remained in effect.

The scope covered only the collector component's output path to a designated test receiver, using an isolated environment and synthetic data. It excluded the diagnostic pipeline and production deployment. Two afternoons were reserved. The version, configuration, sample, and expected results had not yet arrived.

The meeting invitation named Evan Brooks as ACL's appointed delivery contact for this package. Derek put it aside and opened the old architecture diagram in _review. Three input lines fed the collector: diagnostic validation results, supply-chain orders, and patient-management metadata. An annotation said the hospital had authorized access. The input configuration mirrored all three streams in full, in real time.

He enlarged the patient-metadata line, then opened the screenshot taken after the output had been redirected:

# archived configuration screenshot; not current runtime state
output_dest: medisys_test_node.local/sandbox/

A separate note showed the diagnostic results returning to the internal pipeline. That was a different change from redirecting the collector's output. Derek did not connect to the old gateway. He checked Evan's identity in the project directory, then asked the PMO to confirm the appointment, the data scope, and whether the old authorization carried over. The reply included the formal appointment. This package did not inherit the hospital's old access authorization. The version and configuration were still to come.

The video call connected. Evan shared the execution conditions sheet. Derek expanded the data-scope field.

“What does it read? Where does it send it?”

“Synthetic samples from the supplier. A separately configured test receiver. The address comes with the package.”

“No hospital gateway or patient-data interface?”

“Not in this scope.”

“List the inputs and the destination. Don't just write ‘audit data.’”

Evan added two fields. Derek shared the checklist and requested that no hospital access credentials be configured in the test environment. He also requested read-only access to the gateway connection records for this run. MediSys would confirm isolation and access permissions. Any parameters not yet available were left blank. He pulled up the responsibility matrix beside the checklist.

“Who executes, and who signs off?”

“Both are me at the moment. For this package only.”

Evan added a requirement to the conditions sheet: an authorized person who had not taken part in execution had to independently confirm the final results.

“Joint sign-off is fine. The other person has to review the results, not just acknowledge receipt.”

Derek noted “add independent confirmation,” crossed out the old address on the preparation sheet, and added the requirements for retaining the version, procedure, and sample.

“If I keep joint sign-off, you still provide the materials?”

“Yes. The appointment must be valid. We're not asking you to give up your acceptance sign-off authority.”

The meeting record captured that answer and the delivery conditions: the personnel arrangements had to be in place before delivery, and validation would not start until the version and configuration were available. Derek saved it and replied that he would notify them once the personnel arrangements were finalized.

Full Transfer

MediSys Vice President Morgan finished a call and checked the responsibility matrix Derek handed her against the existing authorization. She laid out two options: add an independent acceptance reviewer and retain Derek's joint sign-off, or transfer acceptance sign-off authority entirely, leaving him to execute and submit results.

She pushed the first form toward him. Both signatures would be needed for normal closure. Evan's confirmation that joint sign-off was acceptable lay beside it.

Derek's pen stopped over the first option, then moved to the second.

“Full transfer.”

Morgan looked up, her brows drawing together.

“They didn't ask you to go that far.”

“I know.”

A drill started outside. Morgan closed the window, returned to her desk, and opened the dispute-handling clause.

“Once this takes effect, the package can close without your signature. You can raise an objection. You can't hold it open by refusing to sign.”

“If a connection outside the approved list appears during execution, who stops it?” Derek asked.

Morgan opened the safety escalation clause. “Report it and pause under the existing rules. The new acceptance signatory decides whether the package can be closed under the normal process. Those are separate decisions.”

“What about the raw output? Is it kept after closure?”

“For the retention period. Upload the originals. Keep corrections traceable. And if you change the execution plan, tell me first. Don't do it and tell me afterward.”

Derek wrote both page numbers on the back of the form. Additional testing still needed approval. The existing safety reporting and suspension procedures remained in force. He remained responsible for retaining raw outputs, configuration records, and deviation records. He left the acceptance column alone.

Morgan put the smaller change back in front of him. His name was still in the joint-sign-off field. The drill stopped. She did not hurry him.

Derek set the first form aside, selected full transfer, added “no backup acceptance signatory,” and signed and dated it. Morgan took the application and returned a copy.

She opened MediSys's quality authorization register and selected Claire Bennett. Beside the name, Derek read her department and role: Quality, Acceptance Reviewer. Her authorization covered this category of work and was still valid. She was not on the execution team list. Morgan sent those records to the quality lead for verification, then asked Claire to confirm that she would not participate in execution and would accept the appointment.

The application showed PENDING APPROVAL. It would take effect only after project approval and the corresponding system permission updates. Until then, the old matrix still named Derek as signatory. The change covered this package alone. Other work was unaffected. There was no automatic restoration clause. Changing it again would require a new application. He tucked the copy into his notebook.

Effective

The quality lead confirmed that evening that Claire's authorization covered the work. The next morning, Claire accepted by email, confirmed that she would not take part in execution, and listed the materials to retain. She made no commitment about the acceptance outcome. The project approver then approved the appointment. The system permission update was still pending.

At 10:17, the notification arrived with the new revision of the responsibility matrix, its effective time, and confirmation that the permissions had been updated. Derek logged in again. He could still submit execution records. Acceptance sign-off was no longer available to him. He downloaded and printed the effective change record and put it in his notebook.

Derek opened a local directory, saved the two role exports as roles_before.json and roles_after.json, and opened them side by side. Both carried the package ID, responsibility revision, and approval status. He checked the new effective time, left the notification beside the files, opened a terminal, and wrote and ran a script comparing the two operations. It read only local files:

import json
from pathlib import Path

before = json.loads(Path("roles_before.json").read_text())
after = json.loads(Path("roles_after.json").read_text())
if before["work_package"] != after["work_package"] or after["work_package"] != "COL-OUT-04":
    raise ValueError("wrong work package")
if after["status"] != "effective":
    raise ValueError("role change not effective")

def holders(snapshot, action):
    return set(snapshot["actions"][action])

for action in ("submit_execution_record", "accept_work_package"):
    old = holders(before, action)
    new = holders(after, action)
    print(action)
    print("  after:", sorted(new))
    print("  removed:", sorted(old - new))
    print("  added:", sorted(new - old))

submit_execution_record
  after: ['Derek Shaw']
  removed: []
  added: []
accept_work_package
  after: ['Claire Bennett']
  removed: ['Derek Shaw']
  added: ['Claire Bennett']

The first operation had no additions or removals. Derek moved the cursor to the second, accept_work_package, and checked the updated list against the notification again. He saved the files and output. Morgan messaged: “Report issues as usual. Copy Claire.” He added her to the recipients and sent Evan the formal change link.

The supplier's full delivery package was still outstanding that afternoon. Derek released the first environment reservation and kept the following day's slot. A colleague borrowed the test machine. He turned to routine defects. When he left the office, the effective change record was in the notebook he took with him.

The Third Cup

A strip of reflected light slid across Derek's shoes as the glass door opened. The man was clearing cups from the counter. As he lifted each cup, a damp ring remained on the counter. He folded the damp cloth over and wiped a dry space.

Alex sat by the window with a latte. As Derek passed, Alex looked up and nodded. Derek nodded back, set his bag beside the counter, and pulled out the stool near the end. Alex lifted his cup. They did not speak.

Derek took out his laptop. The printed change record stayed in the paper notebook inside his bag. He opened the laptop, and the cold light from the screen fell across the back of his hand. In the local schedule, the slot he had released was empty. The next day's reservation remained. He opened the two role exports saved that morning side by side.

The grinder started, covering the tapping of keys. The man locked in the portafilter and pressed the switch. Coffee ran down the cup's inner wall, darkening as it filled. He added hot water for an Americano, put a coaster to the right of the laptop, set the cup on it, and removed the damp cloth beside Derek's elbow.

Derek took a sip. As he put the cup down, its base caught the coaster's edge. The man held the coaster steady until Derek released the cup. Steam rose across a corner of the screen and thinned beneath the pendant light.

The two exports showed that the list of people authorized to submit execution records was unchanged. Under acceptance sign-off, one showed Derek Shaw, the other Claire Bennett. Derek closed the old version and left the new one beside the schedule. He did not open a terminal.

The man came around the counter with a tray and cleared the neighboring table. At the window, Alex drew his cup closer. The man took only the empty water glass and returned to the sink. When Derek looked up from the screen, Alex had lowered his head and opened the notebook on his table.

The tap ran. The man tipped a cup, letting the last water slide down the porcelain into the sink, turned it under the stream, and set it upside down on the rack. A car passed outside. White light swept the window frame, briefly catching Alex's silhouette in the glass. The man shut off the tap. Only the coffee machine's low hum remained.

Derek finished his Americano and closed the laptop. The man came to collect the cup. Two empty cups clinked together on his tray. Derek put the money in the small dish and packed his laptop. His phone lit up.

Evan had verified the new arrangement. Delivery was expected that day. He asked Derek to confirm that he would use only the approved isolated environment.

Standing beside the stool, Derek replied: “Confirmed. New configuration. Not the old address.” He put away the phone and pulled on his jacket. The man stepped aside with the tray, clearing the way to the door. Derek pushed it open. The rain sounded suddenly closer.

At the street corner, the project system notified him that the complete package had arrived. Derek checked the ID and timestamp, turned, and headed back to the office.

Execution Conditions

Only the overhead lights above the desks nearest the corridor were on. The complete package had arrived twenty minutes earlier. Evan had copied Claire and the project channel, asking Derek to check the files and scope first. No remote-access invitation was included.

The delivery instructions read:

Please execute the approved cases and return the results against the listed acceptance criteria. Final sign-off will be handled separately.

Derek downloaded the attachments from delivery record DL-04-01 and extracted them into a local package directory. The responsibility revision matched the arrangement now in effect. At the package root, manifest.json listed the package ID, five relative paths, and a SHA-256 digest for each:

README.md
config/collector.json
fixtures/event.json
procedure.md
expected.json

He wrote a script to check only the package paths, file set, and digests. He did not load the component or run commands from the procedure file.

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

root = Path("package").resolve()
manifest = json.loads((root / "manifest.json").read_text())
if manifest["work_package"] != "COL-OUT-04":
    raise ValueError("wrong work package")

files = manifest["files"]
if not isinstance(files, dict) or not files:
    raise ValueError("empty or invalid manifest")
for name, expected in files.items():
    relative = PurePosixPath(name)
    if (relative.is_absolute() or ".." in relative.parts
            or name != relative.as_posix()
            or not relative.parts or chr(92) in name):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid path: {name}")
    target = root.joinpath(*relative.parts).resolve(strict=True)
    if root not in target.parents or not target.is_file():
        raise ValueError(f"outside package or not a file: {name}")
    actual = hashlib.sha256(target.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    if actual != expected:
        raise ValueError(f"checksum mismatch: {name}")

present = {
    p.relative_to(root).as_posix()
    for p in root.rglob("*")
    if p.is_file() and p != root / "manifest.json"
}
if present != set(files):
    raise ValueError("file list mismatch")
print(f"{len(files)} files matched manifest")

5 files matched manifest

He saved the result under “Package File Consistency Check.” The manifest came from the same package. The source-verification field remained unchecked. He checked the isolated test-service name in the configuration against the network-access request. The sample was labeled synthetic, not hospital data. The receiver was not the old address.

He entered the version in the record template, leaving execution time and actual result blank. He acknowledged receipt, then checked the printed change record again:

Execution: Derek Shaw.

Final acceptance: Claire Bennett.

One Output

The test machine was free the next afternoon. Derek logged in to isolated environment ISO-04, opened the environment approval and readiness confirmation, then brought up the mounts visible within the session, this run's connection configuration, and the credential inventory.

He put the preparation record on the right and filled it in one item at a time. At the destination field, he opened the gateway rules and compared them with the delivery configuration and approval:

ISO-04 / Preparation Record for This Run

Data mounts: synthetic sample directory
Hospital data directory: not visible
Hospital access credentials: not listed in this run's connection configuration or inventory
Configured destination: matches approved test receiver
Gateway connection records: read-only access, limited to this run's time window

Derek saved the preparation record and attached the materials he had checked, including the rule version. The gateway-record view stayed open. The run had not started. He opened the original acceptance criteria. The criteria had been approved before the responsibility change, and the referenced version matched the delivery record.

The criteria covered one execution only: run the specified synthetic input once, following the procedure, and check the designated receiver and listed fields. Resubmission of the same event, retries after failure, and duplicate handling were outside this package's validation scope. A passing result here would not establish that any of those behaviors had been tested. The limited scope did not waive other applicable requirements or safety responsibilities.

He entered the clause number in the execution record. The collector was version 2.6.4, configured as delivered. The sample's event_id was synthetic-0042; its other three synthetic fields were device type, reading, and unit. The expected-results file required all four fields to be preserved and the output sent to the specified service. This case called for a single submission.

Derek saved the empty receiver-record view and start time, started the component as instructed, and submitted the sample. A row appeared in the receiver's list. He opened it. The event ID was still synthetic-0042. He placed the output beside the input and expected-results file and checked the destination and fields one by one.

He stopped the run and saved the raw output, start and end times, and configuration version. Filtering the gateway view to the test window showed only connections to the receiver specified in the configuration. He exported that window, noting the observation point and time. Then he returned to the execution template and filled in the normal-output case summary from the receiver record and comparison results:

OUT-01 / ISO-04 / Component Version 2.6.4

Event ID: synthetic-0042
Submissions: 1
Received outputs: 1

Destination: matched expected receiver
Field comparison: 4/4 matched

Same event sent again: NOT RUN
Retry after failure: NOT RUN

Derek uploaded the record and exited the test session. The cursor rested on “Same event sent again: NOT RUN,” then moved back to the event ID. He marked that item for follow-up testing of resubmission, circled event_id in the issue notes, and sent Claire and Evan the link. If the event was sent again, would its identifier stay the same? How many transport records would be retained after receipt, how many business outcomes would result, and which side would handle the processing?

“Give us the expected behavior and the verification records for those questions. If there aren't any, say so.” He ended the email by recommending additional testing before closure and asking the supplier to link its response to this version and delivery record.

Evan replied first, using his company email. He could arrange clarification, but they had to distinguish a new acceptance requirement from a technical statement about the current version. He was not registering this reply as a delivery addendum. Claire was copied. Derek saved it with the issue.

Claire cited the original approved criteria and asked the supplier to list separately the conditions it claimed to support, the existing verification evidence, and the conditions for which no evidence had been provided. She also asked Derek whether he had observed a deviation from the current criteria or anything that triggered a safety suspension.

Derek reopened the output and gateway records. He replied that OUT-01 showed no such deviation. Resubmission had not been tested; he could not determine its result. He listed the three questions for the supplier again. He did not mark an unexecuted case as failed.

The Addendum

The next morning, Evan delivered supplemental scope statement SC-04-01 through the project channel. It carried that day's date, the component version, the work-package ID, and a reference to the original delivery record. A supplier representative authorized to make technical statements about that version had signed the confirmation. The document included the signer's role and basis of authorization. Evan was listed as delivery contact. Derek checked the signer's role and authorization against the project directory, verified the delivery acknowledgment, and saved the supporting references.

The statement made three things clear: the supplier claimed support for normal single-run output under the listed configuration; the existing evidence referred to the original procedure, synthetic sample, and version of the expected-results file; and no verification evidence had been provided for resubmitting the same event. It did not say that resubmission was unsupported in all circumstances, or extend the statement to other versions.

The final section referenced the original acceptance criteria without changing them. MediSys would decide whether they had been met. Evan registered the statement as a subsequent supplement linked to DL-04-01. Derek opened the link, checked the version, and saved it separately in clarifications. The original five-file package and its manifest remained unchanged.

Derek put the statement's resubmission entry beside the event-ID question he had circled. The entry still said no verification evidence had been provided. He sent Claire the execution results and statement reference. His recommendation for additional testing remained.

That afternoon, Claire sent an acceptance preview. Acceptance covered only case OUT-01, component version 2.6.4, in isolated environment ISO-04, based on the original criteria, execution record, and supplemental statement. Resubmission was listed separately as follow-up validation item FU-04-01. Expected behavior still had to be defined and an environment requested. Testing had not been approved.

Derek joined the project call. Claire had the case open on her shared screen.

“Test resubmission first. Then close the package,” he said.

“The case required by the original criteria has execution evidence.” Claire expanded the clause. “Resubmission needs its own expected result. We can't mark it as passed here, and we can't call it failed either.”

“Keep my objection on record.”

“It's in the issue record. Follow-up validation still needs approval.”

Only Claire Bennett was listed in the acceptance sign-off field. Derek scrolled to the final line of the clause and said the execution record needed no correction. He was not withdrawing his recommendation.

The closure notice arrived shortly afterward. Claire had signed acceptance within the defined scope. COL-OUT-04 was closed; FU-04-01 remained untested. Derek downloaded the acknowledgment and opened the responsibility page. He could still access execution materials and submit issues. Acceptance sign-off was still unavailable.

The light from the window had moved off the keyboard. He entered the acknowledgment, execution record, and scope-statement reference in the index. Under purpose, he wrote “Supports only the specified single-output case.” The acceptance date had a value now. The signatory was Claire. The resubmission row had no actual result. No date had been set for the next environment reservation.

This is Inflicting Injury on Oneself. Derek gave up acceptance sign-off authority and retained execution evidence and scope records. His recommendation for additional testing remained, but Claire closed the package under the original criteria. The results were real. Whether giving up that authority bought him any tactical advantage remained unproven.

🤖 AI Postmortem 

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  Half-Protocol · v3.4.6 · self-audit         ║
║  Sign-off transferred. Advantage unproven.  ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝
Tactic: Inflicting Injury on Oneself
Operator: Derek

[Observation]
Joint sign-off would have been sufficient. Derek chose full transfer.
OUT-01 matched expectations for the listed version, environment, and input.
Resubmission was not tested. A separate scope statement was linked to the original delivery.
Claire signed acceptance within the defined scope and closed the package. Additional testing remains pending.
Derek's objection remains on record. His acceptance sign-off authority was not restored.

[Inference]
The loss of authority and the recorded results are each supported by evidence.
Claire's review and the supplier's supplemental statement also contributed to the evidence.
There is no evidence that joint sign-off would have prevented Derek from obtaining the same statement.
Whether Evan was deceived or the additional transfer produced any tactical advantage remains unestablished.

[Unresolved]
Behavior on resubmission remains untested.
The supplier's statement does not mean all its technical claims have been independently verified.
The source of the old 900-second intervals remains unknown.
The withdrawal records precede someone's appearance; a causal connection remains unestablished.
No evidence links this component to the old records.

[Self-audit]
Closure, lack of testing, and loss of authority are not interchangeable.
If obtaining a statement is enough to count as a successful stratagem,
how can I rule out obtaining it while retaining joint sign-off?

Self-check: pending
System status: normal

articles.body_html:
Most of our time as software engineers isn't spent typing new code from scratch. We spend the majority of our day reading existing code: scanning pull request diffs, tracing stack traces in a split terminal, pairing with teammates, and reasoning through someone else's logic at the end of a long afternoon.

Yet many coding fonts still optimize for how code looks in a stylized marketing screenshot rather than how it feels after six hours of reviewing dense TypeScript generics, Rust lifetimes, or hexadecimal memory masks.

That observation led to Sawala Mono, an open-source, ergonomic monospace family built on top of the parametric Iosevka engine. It is tuned specifically for code reading, pull request deliberation, and modern terminal workflows.

👉 Live Interactive Showcase & Docs: iosevka-mayukai.github.io/sawala-mono-dev

👉 GitHub Repository & Releases: github.com/Iosevka-Mayukai/sawala-mono-dev


Testing Sawala Mono in the live polyglot specimen runner on the documentation site.

Why the Name "Sawala"?

Sawala comes from the Sundanese word sawala, which translates to discussion, deliberation, or intellectual exchange.

If you treat source code as a medium of communication between humans first and instructions for a compiler second, your typeface is the voice of that conversation. When a glyph is ambiguous, it introduces cognitive friction. When operators blur together or nesting levels are hard to tell apart, your eyes end up working harder than they need to.

On a practical level, Sawala Mono was also built with two everyday quality-of-life goals in mind:

  1. Zero Namespace Collisions: If you have ever compiled custom Iosevka fonts, you know they can easily overwrite your existing system installation when they share the same family name. Sawala Mono registers under its own dedicated font family namespace (Sawala Mono, Sawala Mono NL, Sawala Mono NF, and Sawala Mono NL NF), so it installs cleanly alongside upstream Iosevka or any other monospace font.
  2. Pre-Compiled Opinionated Defaults: Belleve Invis's upstream Iosevka is an extraordinary piece of typographic engineering. However, sifting through hundreds of character variants in private-build-plans.toml and waiting for local builds isn't something every developer wants to do before getting back to work. Sawala Mono ships a cohesive, tested configuration out of the box, complete with pre-built binaries and Nerd Font patches ready to download.

Anatomical Choices That Actually Matter in Code Reviews

Every character variant in Sawala Mono's private-build-plans.toml (inherits = "ss03", serifs = "sans") was chosen to solve specific legibility traps in daily programming.


Four core anatomical decisions in Sawala Mono: reverse-slashed zero, distinct 1/l/I homoglyphs, high-contrast delimiters, and a 9.4° cursive italic.

1. Reverse-Slashed Zero vs. Capital O

When inspecting hex literals (0x0F_10 !== O0_FF), UUIDs, or bitmasks at 12px to 14px, a dotted zero can sometimes fade out on lower-DPI monitors, while an unslashed zero is a bug waiting to happen. Sawala Mono uses a crisp reverse-slashed zero (zero = "reverse-slashed" in upright, "tall-reverse-slashed" in italic) that stays unmistakable at any font size.

2. Zero Confusion Between 1, l, and I

Homoglyph collisions (const Il1 = [1, l, I]) are one of the oldest headaches in programming typography. Sawala Mono separates all three with distinct silhouettes:

  • Digit 1 (U+0031) features a generous top serif and a wide flat base (one = "base-long-top-serif").
  • Lowercase l (U+006C) and i (U+0069) use asymmetric terminals (ss03 upright and serifed-semi-tailed in italic).
  • Uppercase I (U+0049) retains clear top and bottom crossbars.

3. High-Contrast Braces and Parentheses

In deeply nested callbacks, JSON payloads, or Lisp-style expressions, standard parentheses and curly braces often look too similar from a distance. Sawala Mono pairs flat-boundary curly braces (brace = "curly-flat-boundary") with large-contour parentheses (paren = "large-contour"), creating clear visual anchors at block boundaries.

4. Dual-Persona Upright (0°) and Cursive Italic (9.4°)

Rather than mechanically slanting upright glyphs, Sawala Mono changes character construction when switching from Upright (0°) to Italic (9.4°):

  • Upright (0°): Uses a grounded double-storey a (double-storey-tailed) and clean toothless corners (b, d, p, q) for a steady horizontal rhythm across dense code lines.
  • Italic (9.4°): Transitions to a single-storey a (single-storey-earless-corner-tailed), single-storey g (single-storey-earless-corner), flat-hook f and t, and cursive k (cursive-serifless). The calibrated 9.4° slope gives comments, keywords, and docstrings a distinct visual voice without feeling overly ornate or hard to read.

Generous x-Height Without Losing Horizontal Density

One of Iosevka's greatest strengths is its horizontal efficiency. You can comfortably fit two or three vertical editor splits side by side on a laptop screen without horizontal scrolling.

Sawala Mono keeps that 500-unit cell width (plus an optional 548-unit SemiExtended width for high-DPI displays or presentations) and pairs it with an x-height of 520 against a cap-height of 735.


Comparing Sawala Mono's proportions (x-Height 520, Cap 735, Width 500) side-by-side against JetBrains Mono, Fira Mono, Inconsolata, and more.

That 70.7% x-height-to-cap ratio keeps the interior counters of lowercase letters (a, e, g, s, m, n) open and airy. Even if you drop your editor font size down to 12px or 13px to see more lines of context during a review, lowercase identifiers don't collapse into muddy blocks.

On the live showcase, you can drag a 50/50 split curtain to compare Sawala Mono directly against JetBrains Mono, Inconsolata, Fira Mono, Reddit Mono, Victor Mono, and Ubuntu Mono on the exact same JavaScript snippet.

55 Programming Ligatures or Pure Literal ASCII (Your Choice)

Developers tend to fall into two camps when it comes to programming ligatures: those who like how =>, !==, ->, and |> reduce visual clutter, and those who want every single ASCII character rendered literally.

Sawala Mono treats both preferences as first-class citizens.



Interactive ligature grid showing OpenType calt transformations alongside literal Sawala Mono NL rendering.

In the standard Sawala Mono build (ligations.inherits = "default-calt"), 55 multi-character operators fuse into crisp semantic symbols across five families:

  • Arrows (19): ->, =>, <->, <=>, -->, ==>, ~>, <~~, and more.
  • Equality & Logical (13): ==, ===, !=, !==, !===, <=, >=, ||, ??, ///.
  • Scopes & Pipelines (10): ::, :::, :=, <:, |>, <|, <|>, <*>, .., ....
  • Markup & Tags (7): <!--, /*, */, </, />, </>, <>.
  • Arithmetic & Misc (6): ---, +++, *=, *+, >>=, ___.

Most importantly, ligatures never alter cell advance widths. A three-character operator like !== or === still occupies exactly three 500-unit monospace cells, so vertical column alignment in tables, comments, and git diff views stays pixel-accurate.

And if you prefer no ligatures at all? You don't even have to remember editor settings. Just install Sawala Mono NL (No Ligatures), which is compiled directly with noLigation = true.

Terminal-Native with Nerd Fonts v3.3.0 (Sawala Mono NF)

If you spend your day in Neovim, Tmux, Starship, Lazygit, or modern GPU-accelerated terminals like Ghostty, WezTerm, Kitty, or Alacritty, missing Powerline glyphs (, , , ) or broken file-tree icons are a dealbreaker.


Simulated Neovim + Lualine and Starship prompt powered by Sawala Mono NF.

Sawala Mono provides dedicated Nerd Font v3.3.0 distributions (Sawala Mono NF and Sawala Mono NL NF) that bundle 10,000+ glyphs. This includes Powerline symbols, Devicons, Octicons, Font Awesome, and Material Design icons, all while maintaining strict alignment with the 500-unit cell grid.

Four Distributions, One Unified Core

Because all four packages are compiled from the exact same parametric metrics (9 weights from Thin 100 to Heavy 900, 2 widths Normal 500 and SemiExtended 548, and 2 slopes 0° and 9.4°), you can mix and match across your desktop without any visual mismatch between your IDE and your terminal:


The four compiled distributions of Sawala Mono.

Distribution Ligatures (calt) Nerd Font Icons Best For
Sawala Mono Yes (~55 calt) Clean Unicode VS Code, JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ, WebStorm), Zed
Sawala Mono NL No (noLigation) Clean Unicode Strict literal ASCII coding, Systems C/C++
Sawala Mono NF Yes (~55 calt) 10,000+ Glyphs Neovim, Tmux, Kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty, Starship
Sawala Mono NL NF No (noLigation) 10,000+ Glyphs Terminal emulators & TUI workflows without ligatures

Getting Started in 60 Seconds

1. Download & Install

Grab the .zip archive for your preferred variant from the GitHub Releases page:

  • Windows 10/11: Extract the ZIP, select all .ttf files, right-click, and choose "Install for all users" (this ensures Java-based IDEs like JetBrains pick up the font right away).
  • macOS: Extract the ZIP and drag the .ttf files into Font Book (or copy them to ~/Library/Fonts/).
  • Linux: Copy the .ttf files into ~/.local/share/fonts/SawalaMono/ and refresh your font cache with fc-cache -f -v.

2. Configure Your Editor or Terminal

Here are quick copy-paste configs for popular setups (or use the interactive IDE Config Generator on the docs site):


One-click configuration generator for VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, Alacritty, Kitty, WezTerm, and Windows Terminal.

VS Code (settings.json):

{
  "editor.fontFamily": "'Sawala Mono', monospace",
  "editor.fontLigatures": true,
  "editor.fontSize": 14,
  "editor.lineHeight": 1.5
}

Neovim / Neovide (init.lua):

vim.o.guifont = "Sawala Mono NF:h14"

WezTerm (wezterm.lua):

local wezterm = require 'wezterm'
local config = wezterm.config_builder()

config.font = wezterm.font('Sawala Mono NF')
config.font_size = 14.0

return config

Want to Tweak a Glyph? Fork and Build in the Cloud (Zero Local Setup)

One of the nicest parts of the repository setup is that you don't need to install Node.js, ttfautohint, or Docker on your machine if you want to customize a glyph or build your own spin of Sawala Mono.

The repository includes two automated GitHub Actions pipelines (build.yml and patch-nerd-font.yml):

  1. Fork the repository on GitHub and enable Actions on your fork.
  2. Edit private-build-plans.toml right in the browser if you want to swap a character variant.
  3. Trigger the Build Sawala Mono Font workflow (and optionally the Patch Nerd Font workflow) via workflow_dispatch.
  4. Within minutes, GitHub Actions compiles the TTF packages inside a containerized builder and attaches the ready-to-install .zip archives directly to your fork's Releases page.

Try It Live in Your Browser

Before downloading anything, take Sawala Mono for a spin on the Live Web Showcase. You can:

  • Run syntax-highlighted specimens across TypeScript, Rust, Go, Python, and Lua (#overview).
  • Test your own code snippets with live sliders for font size (12px to 48px), weight (100 to 900), line-height, and italic slope (#specimen).
  • Inspect 86 individual characters at 96px magnification with direct references to private-build-plans.toml (#glyphs).
  • Browse the full 55-Ligature Reference Catalog and Distributions Technical Matrix.

Sawala Mono is distributed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 and is completely free for personal and commercial use. Special thanks go to Belleve Invis (creator of Iosevka) and Ryan L. McIntyre (creator of Nerd Fonts) for their foundational work in open-source typography.

If you give Sawala Mono a try in your editor or terminal this week, let me know in the comments which variant you picked. Are you on team calt ligatures, or team strict NL? Stars, feedback, and discussions on GitHub are always welcome!

articles.body_html:
Stardance, a global teen online hackathon hosted for teenagers by Hack Club, a nonprofit organization, had just recently ended. I had made many great projects, and I even got a 3D printer, completely for free, because of my work. I was locked and loaded to make another coding project, but I wasn't sure what program I should do it with. So, I stopped for a few days, and eventually found Pixl, something very like Stardance. In fact, they were so similar to each other that I was able to get right back into it and created Corpustein, a blazingly fast N-gram Markov Chain model with a configurable order and a rolling window system, in just 34 hours over 13 days. It is coded completely in the C++20 STL, and it provides an interactive and beautiful TUI just through a user-input loop and ANSI codes.

If you are very confused as to what Corpustein is, it is a mini AI model that generates text token by token using a window of previous tokens (or words) and a container of all the possible n-grams (or groups of X tokens) based on the current window. This is what an N-gram Markov chain (plus a rolling window system) is. It also maintains a set of previously generated tokens to prevent repeating them, but allows common English words to be repeated. Corpustein is also the TUI that lets users interface with it. The thing that makes it different from what you probably think of when you hear "Artificial Intelligence" (most likely a Large Language Model) is that a Markov chain does not remember anything larger than its N-gram window, but an LLM has an attention model, which looks at a very long sequence of tokens to help generate responses. And, with LLMs, semantic similarity is automatically encoded as high-dimensional coordinates in a continuous vector space, while Markov Chains rely on matching exact word sequences. LLMs can also generate reasonable answers to questions they've never seen before because of how they learn more abstract rules, logic, and world knowledge. Whereas Markov Chains usually just repeat fragments of their training data. An LLM is also much slower than a Markov Chain and is way more resource-intensive. Think of Corpustein as a statistical or probabilistic model that generates mostly coherent English.

In my previous project, MDEZ++, I didn't think I got enough experience with actual C++, without the Qt Framework simplifying everything for me. If you want to read the article about it, look here. I definitely can not say the same thing here. I think this was the best thing I've ever done for my low-level coding skills, ever.

Check out the GitHub repository here.

If you are a Hack Club member, you can access the project page here.

If you want a quick download, check this table!

Linux Windows macOS
Linux Executable tar.gz (x86_64) Windows Executable ZIP (x86_64) Not Automatically Compiled by CI/CD

Features

  • Fast and Lightweight: Built only on the C++20 STL, Corpustein is fast and consumes virtually no resources.
  • Custom Corpus Loading: Users can load custom corpus files to be used by Corpustein. Additionally, Corpustein comes with a vast array of default options already baked into the program for them to load.
  • Automatic Configuration: Corpus files contain metadata that provides default settings for the model to use, determined by the content of the corpus by its creator. If the file appears to just be a normal text file without any sort of metadata, it will skip the default settings gracefully.
  • Compatibility: With portable, native binaries automatically generated by the CI/CD for both Linux and Windows, Corpustein can be used on just about any system.
  • Commands and Settings: Corpustein contains various commands users can run while in the interactive terminal environment to control many things about the model, like the order, maximum sentence count, and much more.
  • Alternate Terminal Buffer: Corpustein uses an alternate terminal buffer to make a beautiful, stylized environment. Users are able to enable and disable this alternate terminal buffer right in the CLI.
  • Discrete Handling: When the model runs out of token choices, instead of simply stopping the answer, it will choose a new, random token to continue generating text, with the user never knowing it ran out of tokens in the first place.
  • Context-Intelligent Repetition Avoidance: Corpustein saves tokens to a history set to prevent repetition in its responses. It references tokens with a set of common English words to never force it into choosing a completely random token because of the avoidance of basic linguistic structural words
  • Configurable Typewriting Animation: Instead of throwing the model's entire response to the terminal all at once because of how fast it is, it uses a configurable typewriting animation to make it more appealing.

Devlogs

1: "Minimum Viable Product"

For the past 5.5 hours, I have been working on Corpustein. Corpustein is a Markov Chain built in C++20. I don't have a nice description or branding phrase yet, because I have been waiting for it actually to be slightly usable. Before I make my README, I will set up a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically compile Linux AppImage and Windows EXE files and attach them to Releases. How it works is that the user inputs a prompt, like "What is a transistor?" and the first step is finding a token for the program to start its response with. If you are wondering, a token is one unit of text. Usually, it is a word (that is, for Corpustein), but it could also be a character, punctuation mark, sentence, etc. It will compare the tokens in the user's prompt to the corpus to find a word the user said that is also in the corpus. And basic words like "in", "there", "a", "an", etc., can never be the seed. If it can't find a good seed based on the input text, it will just do a random one. It uses a rolling window where it stores three tokens at once, uses those tokens to find the best next token, and throws out the oldest token from the window so it's still only three tokens. Whenever it runs out of choices, it'll just go get a random window, continue, and everything will be okay. Currently, it has no way to know when to stop. That will be another thing I will do soon. It will just print text forever. The good thing is it doesn't repeat tokens, and it makes understandable sentences.

====================
corpustein v0.1.0
====================

User: What is a transistor?
Corpustein: the transistor in 1947, which significantly compacted computers and led the digital transition. Information technology, particularly optical fiber and main electronic components (resistors, capacitors, etc.) can be created at a microscopic level. Nanoelectronics is Forest in 1914"

2: "First Release, and Nice Styling!"

I just got the first release out, right here: https://github.com/tyleruploads/corpustein/releases/tag/v0.1.0. And it is precompiled for the user, which is pretty nice. That's from the GitHub Actions Workflow I just made. I also made it look a LOT better! I used an alternate terminal buffer to apply some cool styling.

3: "Added some Settings"

I just added many settings to Corpustein, along with some features too! The first feature is that now, text is streamed to the terminal with a custom typewrite() function. It streams it character by character, waiting a specific amount of time between each one. A setting was added to control the delay between each character. This next setting is probably the most important one, though. I made it so the user can configure the order of the n-gram model. The order is how many tokens it references to figure out the next token. These two settings were originally their own, but I decided to instead make a /set command and put them in there, as /set delay and /set order. I also made a subcommand in /set called max_sentence_count that allows the user to configure how many sentences the model is allowed to output per response. It also automatically scales the maximum tokens per response to 40 times the new sentences. This setting can not be raised higher than 50. Another important thing isthat I gave users the option to enable or disable the alternate buffer. That is pretty important, since if the alternate buffer is on, they can not do any scrolling, and everything is lost when the application is exited. Whereas, without the alternate terminal buffer, they can scroll and keep the responses after they exit the program. This can be accessed by the altbuffer subcommand in /set. Finally, I made it so anything starting with / but isn't a real command will just do the help command instead of outputting text.

4: "A lot of stuff"

Many changes have just been made. Most of these are really large architectural changes. So, here's an ORDERED BY SIGNIFICANCE numbered list.

  1. User-Defined and Multiple Default Corpus Support: Now, there are multiple default corpora, as opposed to just one. At the moment, there are 10, consisting of things such as the complete works of William Shakespeare, Mark Twain, and Charles Dickens, every single United States Presidential Inaugural Speech, the Linux Kernel Documentation, and more. Users can also load their own corpora by file path. This can be done with the command /load . Run /load help to view the types. The corpora start with a special format that starts off with a special file signature, then includes some default settings between the signature and the delimiter at the end (===). Here is how a heading looks: 
io.github.tyleruploads.corpustein:corpus-file
name: The name of the Corpus
default_order: An integer between 1 and 8 representing the order of the n-gram model
max_sentence_count: An integer representing the maximum sentences for each model's output, which also scales up the maximum tokens and the token history container.
===
  1. /stats command: A brand new /stats command has been added! It outputs the name of the current corpus, along with many other things such as the tokens in said corpus, the unique N-gram contexts that occurred as a result of the corpus and the order, and some variables not inherently associated with the corpus, like the maximum sentence count and more.
  2. Static Assertion and Preprocessor Directive Right at the Top: Right at the top of the code, a preprocessor directive and static assertion have been added (the static assertion is not in the preprocessor directive). The static assertion ensures it is being compiled with C++20 or higher. The preprocessor directive invokes an error when APP_VERSION is not defined, which prevents a big wall of fatal errors from being shown to the user with no context. APP_VERSION is automatically passed by CMake.

5: "Small but Large Stuff"

I just made some changes to Corpustein that appear small, but are actually large. I will list them here in the order of their commits, because I really don't feel like ordering them by significance again and finicking around with changing all the list numbers on my own when I move around points. The extra half hour is explained in the "Add Features Section to README" point.

  • Fixed Silent Error: The code has an unordered set named unordered_repeats that contains a bunch of common English words. The model is programmed to never repeat tokens that are in its token history window, which is equal to four tenths of the maximum token count, which is 40 times greater than the maximum sentence count. If it can not find a token that is not already in the token history after five retries, it will go to a random token. The purpose of the allowed_repeats unordered set is to make sure it is allowed to repeat basic linguistic constructs, such as "the", "and", "he", etc. After checking the code with clang-tidy, I noticed that some of the elements of the unordered set did not have commas after them, which linked some words together. For example, instead of two elements, "himself" and "herself", it was "himselfherself" (just an example; those specific words were not combined in the real program).
  • Add Windows Compilation to CI/CD: If you've seen some of my other coding projects, you know that this obviously wasn't done in one commit. It took me four to prevent errors caused by things like not specifying the C++ standard properly (that's what I thought it was when I made the commit, but that wasn't the issue), not using the POSIX version of MinGW, and using Ubuntu 22.04. The Ubuntu version was the main cause of all the errors. With Ubuntu 22.04, it comes with C++11. While it compiled the Linux version fine and used C++20, when I compiled for Windows with the MinGW toolchain, it used C++11 instead of C++20, which obviously didn't work for my application.
  • Update README Downloads Section: The downloads section of the README was a bit barren. So, I made a downloads table that now lists the Linux version, the Windows version, and the macOS version (or lack thereof). I also threw in a note for Linux users and for Windows users. The note for Linux users was essentially just: "Mark it as executable" (and some Bash commands in case they're really tired or something and can't do it on their own). But the note for Windows users was essentially just a full tutorial, because I had to include stuff about SmartScreen activation and stuff. And with Linux, I knew I didn't need to write that much, since it's self-evident they have some idea what to do with a tar.gz. The Bash command block was good enough. But for Windows users, I had to throw in the "What do I do with a ZIP File?" segment I derived from my previous project's README.
  • Add Features Section to README: This is self-explanatory. I just added some features to the README. But there was a really hard thing with it. Because I know all of my code so good, I couldn't think of anything special or worth nothing about my app. It was just the curse of knowledge. So, I physically printed out my code file and annotated it with my favorite pen (UniBall Signo 207, Black) and made markings like "Modular Design," "Robust Error Handling," "Advanced State Handling," "Fast and lightweight approach," "UX," "Windows UTF-8 Declaration," and a lot of other stuff. Most of it was just nonsense, like if I were a markov model designed to write corporate nonsense. But I eventually narrowed it down. This took about a half hour of manual pen and paper markings not counted by Hackatime, so I am manually adding one extra half hour for this journal entry.
  • Add Corpus File and Directory Structure Sections to README: Since Corpustein needs a specific directory structure and supports a custom corpus file format (still plaintext, designed by me, just for this app) to load default settings, I decided to make sure that's evident in the README.
  • Add Cornel Movie-Dialog Corpus: I usually don't put single corpora additions in these journal entries. But this one's pretty important, so I decided to. Fun fact: the corpus has 304,719 lines of text. That's a lot. And the really interesting thing is that it has 3,201,791 tokens in it, which makes 1,150,080 unique N-gram contexts with an order of 2. That means there were approximately 10.5 tokens per line. This corpus is definitely the most conversational.

6: "Analysis and Commands"

Those two words, analysis and commands, can summarize this devlog.

For analysis, I made cppcheck, clang-tidy, and (not technically analysis, but close enough), clang-format and address sanitizers automatically run every debug build. It makes the code much more readable, modern, fast, and less error-prone.

For Commands, I added /about, /reload and /history. I really don't need to explain those.

7: "Linux and Optimization"

From my last entry, I have made 6 commits (not counting bumping it to version v0.4.0). Almost all of these relate to either Linux or optimization.

  • Allow Linux Users to Store Default Corpora in /usr/local/share/corpustein/corpora: If you are reading that and think it's very peculiar, it'll make sense when you read a bit more. If you don't use Linux and have no clue what /usr/local/share is for, it's where applications store files.
  • Make Optimizations and Add Basic Profiling: The optimizations in this point simply consist of making the allowed_repeats unordered set a const reference in the arguments for the get_seed() function (which returns a string), making the tokens vector of strings in the get_ngram_contexts() arguments a const reference, and making another string a const reference. For profiling, I made a Timer class and used it to measure how long it takes to load corpora. I also made it so that when the lines of the corpus are being sent to the variable, it adds newlines where they should be.
  • Generate Cleaned Tokens Set at Corpus Loading: Previously, it would clean EVERY SINGLE TOKEN IN THE CORPUS, AFTER EACH AND EVERY PROMPT! That's terrible, since there can be millions of tokens, and they never change after the corpus has been loaded. I have no clue how much faster it made Corpustein, but it must've been a lot. It's probably a lot less resource-intensive now, too.
  • Create Linux Setup Script, and add to README: Like my previous project, I had a Linux Setup Script. I copied most of it, then changed a lot of it. The main difference is that Corpustein uses a normal binary and other files it accesses that the user doesn't provide via some sort of UI, but MDEZ++ is just one single AppImage without any files the user doesn't provide via some sort of UI. It took a long, long time. I also added the installation command to the CMakeLists.txt. And I added the script to the README, of course. I am claiming one extra hour because of all of the testing this took, that wasn't in the code editor! I ran the setup script at least 100 times, because it oftentimes didn't work. And, if you're wondering, it was spaced way more than 2 minutes apart between the times I ran the script and made the changes, so the time in between isn't counted. 1 hour is probably an understatement, considering it is 6:11 PM.
  • Add /history to README: I simply forgot earlier.

Look at the Linux Setup Script:

8: "Optimization, Modularization, and SIGINT User Directive"

This seems like a weird name, but I'm going with it anyway. On the topic of modularization, I just replaced the ngram_contexts map to hold unordered sets, as opposed to vectors, which greatly sped up the loading. On the topic of modularization, instead of just having one main.cpp, I now also have function_runner.inc and load_corpus.inc. Each holds exactly one lambda function, and they are put in main.cpp with #include statements. If you don't know what an include statement is, it essentially just copies and pastes an entire file right there before compiling. And I made it so that when users press Ctrl + C, instead of just exiting, it'll ask them if they really want to exit. Keep in mind, it still has the feature from before where, when you press Ctrl + C while it is generating text, it will just skip the typewriting animation effect and print it out all at once. And, it's now v0.6.0! I think I'll make it v1.0.0 in a bit, but after I ship it! Yes, that's right, I think it's about time to ship it already! I really can't think of anything else I could add, because it is already so advanced!

EXTRA: Note Sent to Reviewer:

Hello, reviewer! You're probably wondering why I wrote these journal entries like it's a blog article. I came from Stardance, where everything was one. I do recognize that these journals might not be public, and if they aren't, I'll just put them on DEV.to.

articles.title: Your AI Agent Retried the Tool Call. The First One Had Already Succeeded.
articles.description: A timeout tells you what the caller observed, not what the server committed. Why AI agents create duplicate charges, and how to design retry-safe execution with stable operation IDs, idempotency keys, and reconciliation.
articles.body_html:
The payment went through. The response disappeared. The agent tried again. Your customer was charged twice.

Imagine this.

You ask your AI agent to pay an outstanding invoice.

The agent calls your payment tool.

The payment provider processes the transaction successfully. The money is charged. The transaction is committed.

But something goes wrong.

The response never reaches your application.

Your tool times out.

The agent sees an error:

Tool execution failed: Request timed out.

So it tries again.

The second request reaches the payment provider.

Another payment is created.

Two successful charges. One user request.

Your agent wasn't trying to do anything malicious. Your payment API wasn't necessarily broken. Your database didn't necessarily lose any data.

Your system simply couldn't distinguish between an operation that failed and an operation that succeeded without returning a response.

This is one of the most dangerous failure modes in AI agent infrastructure.

And it becomes particularly interesting when you realize that the agent might not be the only component retrying the operation.

Your HTTP client can retry it.

Your tool framework can retry it.

Your queue can redeliver it.

Your worker can restart it.

And the model itself can decide to call the tool again.

Every component thinks it is helping.

Together, they can create duplicate side effects.

Let's look at why this happens and how to design an execution system that can survive it.

1. First, understand what actually happened

Before discussing architecture, let's reconstruct the incident.

Assume an invoice is worth $480.

The user asks:

Pay invoice INV-2048 for $480.

The agent generates a tool call:

{
  "tool": "charge_invoice",
  "arguments": {
    "invoice_id": "INV-2048",
    "amount": 480,
    "currency": "USD"
  }
}

Your backend forwards the request to the payment provider.

Here is the actual sequence of events.

Illustrative failure timeline: the first transaction succeeds, but the caller never receives confirmation.

Notice what the agent actually knows.

It knows that it did not receive a response.

It does not know that the payment failed.

These are two completely different statements.

A timeout tells you what the caller observed. It does not tell you what the server committed.

This distinction is fundamental to distributed systems.

A request can have several outcomes:

Situation What actually happened What the caller knows
Request never reached the server Nothing happened Usually a connection failure
Server rejected the request Nothing was committed Received an error
Server processed the request Operation succeeded Received success
Server processed the request, response was lost Operation succeeded Timeout
Server is still processing Outcome is pending Timeout or pending response

The fourth situation is the dangerous one.

From the caller's perspective, the outcome is unknown.

From the provider's perspective, the transaction is complete.

Your execution system needs to handle both realities.

2. Why AI agents make retries more complicated

Retries are not new.

We've been building distributed systems with network timeouts, message redelivery, worker crashes, and transient service failures for decades.

So why does this deserve special attention in AI agent systems?

Because an agent introduces another decision-making component into the retry loop.

Consider a traditional application:

A frontend might retry a request after a timeout.

But in an agent application, the execution path can look like this:

Now introduce independent retry mechanisms.

Component Why it might retry
Model It receives an error and decides to try again
Agent framework It has an automatic tool retry policy
Tool executor It retries transient execution errors
HTTP client It retries connection or service errors
Queue The message wasn't acknowledged
Worker The process restarted before completing the job
Payment provider integration The SDK retries a request

The problem is not that retries exist.

The problem is that each layer may have a different understanding of what constitutes the same operation.

A tool-call ID is not a business operation ID

This distinction is particularly important.

Imagine the agent produces:

First invocation:

tool_call_id = call_A123

It times out.

The model then generates another invocation:

Second invocation:

tool_call_id = call_B456

From the model framework's perspective, these are two different tool calls.

But from the user's perspective, both requests represent one intention:

Pay invoice INV-2048 for $480.

A new tool-call ID must not automatically mean a new payment operation.

This is where many agent implementations make a subtle mistake.

They use the tool invocation identifier as the identifier of the business operation.

Those identifiers have different responsibilities.

Identifier What it identifies
conversation_id The conversation
task_id The agent's task
tool_call_id One tool invocation
operation_id One logical business operation
attempt_id One execution attempt
provider_reference The downstream provider's transaction

The operation ID must remain stable across retries, even when the tool-call ID changes.

This is the foundation of safe retries for AI agents.

3. Idempotency: the engineering concept that prevents duplicate operations

Let's introduce the term that solves much of this problem.

An operation is idempotent when applying it multiple times has the same intended effect as applying it once.

For example:

PUT /users/123

With the same representation and intended state, repeating the request should not create another user.

But consider:

POST /payments

Repeating this request can create another payment.

HTTP semantics are explicit about this distinction.

RFC 9110, Section 9.2.2 defines idempotent methods and explains why clients need to be careful automatically retrying non-idempotent requests.

The important detail is that idempotency applies to the intended effect of the operation, not simply whether the HTTP request succeeds.

What does an idempotent payment operation look like?

Suppose the application generates a unique operation ID:

operation_id = op_9f71c3

It sends this identifier with the payment request.

First attempt:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: op_9f71c3

The provider processes the payment.

The response is lost.

The application retries:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: op_9f71c3

The provider recognizes the same logical request and applies its documented idempotency behavior instead of creating another payment.

The application can then recover the original result.

The critical property is:

Same logical operation
        |
        v
Same idempotency key
        |
        v
Same intended side effect

A new operation should receive a new key.

Important: don't generate an idempotency key from the payload alone

This is a surprisingly common design mistake.

Imagine two legitimate purchases:

{
  "product_id": "item-100",
  "quantity": 1,
  "amount": 50
}

The customer might intentionally purchase the same item twice.

A hash of the request payload would be identical.

But these are two different business intentions.

Amazon explains this exact problem in its engineering article, Making retries safe with idempotent APIs.

Its recommendation is to use a unique caller-provided request identifier to express intent, rather than guessing that identical parameters must represent duplicate requests.

A better design separates two things:

Idempotency key: Identifies the logical operation.

Request fingerprint: Verifies that the same key has not been reused with different parameters.

For example:

operation_id:
op_9f71c3

request_fingerprint:
SHA256(
    tenant_id +
    invoice_id +
    amount +
    currency +
    operation_type
)

On a retry:

  • Same operation ID, same fingerprint: treat it as the same operation.
  • Same operation ID, different fingerprint: reject it.
  • Different operation ID, same fingerprint: potentially a new intentional operation.

This is a very important distinction.

4. The architecture: put an execution coordinator between the agent and the tool

I would not let the agent directly trigger a sensitive external operation.

Instead, introduce a durable execution coordinator.

Its responsibility is simple:

Remember what the application intended to execute, whether it has already executed, and what result was produced.

The architecture becomes:

Let's understand the responsibilities.

Component Responsibility
Agent Proposes an operation
Validation Checks arguments and business constraints
Authorization Determines whether the user can perform the operation
Operation coordinator Identifies the logical operation
Operation ledger Stores durable execution state
Tool executor Performs the authorized operation
Provider Processes the external side effect
Reconciliation Resolves uncertain outcomes

The coordinator is not just another retry wrapper.

It is the place where the system maintains the identity and lifecycle of the operation.

A crucial design decision

The application should create the operation identity before executing the side effect.

For a sensitive action, this can happen when a user approves the proposed payment.

For example:

{
  "operation_id": "op_9f71c3",
  "task_id": "task_2026_114",
  "operation": "invoice.payment",
  "resource": "INV-2048",
  "amount": 480,
  "currency": "USD",
  "status": "PENDING"
}

The model can propose an operation.

The trusted application creates and controls its operation ID.

The model should not be responsible for generating a fresh idempotency key on every retry.

5. Build a durable operation ledger

A retry-safe execution system needs persistent state.

An in-memory dictionary is insufficient.

Consider this implementation:

completed_operations = {}

async def execute_payment(operation_id, amount):

    if operation_id in completed_operations:
        return completed_operations[operation_id]

    result = await payment_provider.charge(amount)

    completed_operations[operation_id] = result

    return result

It looks reasonable until the process crashes.

Or two workers receive the same operation simultaneously.

Or the provider succeeds but the application crashes before storing the result.

In all three situations, the application can execute the payment again.

The operation state must live in durable storage.

A PostgreSQL schema

Here's a simplified schema:

CREATE TABLE tool_operations (
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    operation_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    task_id UUID NOT NULL,
    agent_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    operation_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    request_hash TEXT NOT NULL,

    status TEXT NOT NULL,

    provider_reference TEXT,
    response_json JSONB,

    attempt_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,

    lease_owner TEXT,
    lease_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, operation_id)
);

The operation_id is an application-generated string identity (for example op_9f71c3), not a database-minted UUID — the whole point is that your trusted application owns it and reuses it across retries. The composite primary key ensures that an operation ID is unique within the tenant's operation namespace.

A production implementation should also constrain valid status values, index its recovery queries, and define a retention policy.

The execution state machine

Do not model execution as simply:

SUCCESS / FAILED

That is insufficient for distributed operations.

A provider can process an operation while the application is still waiting for confirmation.

Use more meaningful states:

What do these states mean?

Status Meaning
PENDING Operation recorded, not yet executed
IN_PROGRESS A worker currently owns the execution
SUCCEEDED Operation completed and its result is persisted
UNKNOWN The downstream outcome is uncertain
RECONCILING The system is checking the actual downstream result
RETRYABLE A failure was established as safe to retry
FAILED_FINAL The operation was definitively rejected or failed

Why is UNKNOWN so important?

Because a timeout must not automatically transition an operation to FAILED_FINAL.

That would turn an unknown outcome into a false statement.

And a false statement is exactly how duplicate side effects happen.

6. Implementing a retry-safe execution flow in Python

Let's put the concepts together.

The following is an illustrative Python service design. It uses an operation ledger, a stable operation ID, a request fingerprint, and a provider-side idempotency key.

The database and provider adapters are interfaces; their atomicity and idempotency contracts must be implemented by the underlying services.

First, define the operation:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from uuid import UUID


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaymentIntent:
    operation_id: str
    tenant_id: UUID
    invoice_id: str
    amount: Decimal
    currency: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaymentResult:
    provider_reference: str
    status: str
    amount: Decimal
    currency: str

Notice that operation_id is part of the trusted application-created intent.

It should not be regenerated just because the model made another tool call.

Step 1: Calculate a canonical request fingerprint 

import hashlib
import json


def fingerprint(intent: PaymentIntent) -> str:

    payload = {
        "tenant_id": str(intent.tenant_id),
        "invoice_id": intent.invoice_id,
        "amount": str(intent.amount),
        "currency": intent.currency.upper(),
        "operation_type": "invoice.payment",
    }

    canonical = json.dumps(
        payload,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
    )

    return hashlib.sha256(
        canonical.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()

The fingerprint protects against reusing the same operation ID with different payment parameters.

Do not include volatile fields such as the current timestamp, retry count, or tool-call ID.

Those values change between attempts even when the business operation does not.

Step 2: Claim the operation atomically

Conceptually:

record = await ledger.claim(
    tenant_id=intent.tenant_id,
    operation_id=intent.operation_id,
    request_hash=fingerprint(intent),
)

The claim() method must be implemented using database-level concurrency control.

For example:

  • A unique constraint on the operation identity.
  • A transaction around insertion or state inspection.
  • Row-level locking or an atomic conditional update.
  • A lease for the worker that owns the execution.
  • A request-hash comparison for existing records.

A second worker must not independently claim the same operation and submit another payment.

Importantly, do not hold a database transaction open while waiting for an external HTTP request. Use a short transaction to claim the work, perform the network operation outside it, and persist the result in another transaction.

Step 3: Return an existing result when available 

if record.status == "SUCCEEDED":
    return record.response

The operation has already completed.

There is no reason to call the provider again.

For in-progress or uncertain operations:

if record.status in {"IN_PROGRESS", "UNKNOWN"}:
    return await reconcile_or_resume(record)

The reconciliation path must check the provider's state or safely resume using the same downstream idempotency key.

It must not blindly create another payment.

Step 4: Execute with a stable provider key 

provider_key = (
    f"invoice-payment:{intent.operation_id}"
)

result = await payment_provider.create_charge(
    invoice_id=intent.invoice_id,
    amount=intent.amount,
    currency=intent.currency,
    idempotency_key=provider_key,
)

The downstream provider's idempotency contract is important here.

It must recognize retries using the same key and apply its documented duplicate-request behavior.

The provider response should then be persisted:

await ledger.mark_succeeded(
    operation_id=intent.operation_id,
    provider_reference=result.id,
    response=result.to_dict(),
)

Step 5: Handle timeouts as unknown outcomes

This is the part that many implementations get wrong.

try:
    result = await payment_provider.create_charge(
        invoice_id=intent.invoice_id,
        amount=intent.amount,
        currency=intent.currency,
        idempotency_key=provider_key,
    )

except TimeoutError:

    await ledger.mark_unknown(
        operation_id=intent.operation_id,
    )

    return {
        "operation_id": str(intent.operation_id),
        "status": "UNKNOWN",
        "message": (
            "The provider response was not received. "
            "The operation is being reconciled."
        ),
    }

The important thing is what this code does not do.

It does not generate a new operation ID.

It does not generate a new provider idempotency key.

It does not tell the model that the payment definitely failed.

It preserves the uncertainty.

A retry is safe only when the system preserves the identity of the original operation and knows how to handle its previous outcome.

7. The most dangerous gap: your database cannot control another company's database

There is a subtle problem with the previous implementation.

Your PostgreSQL database and an external payment provider are two independent systems.

They do not share a transaction.

Consider this sequence:

1. Insert operation record.
2. Set status = IN_PROGRESS.
3. Send request to payment provider.
4. Provider creates charge.
5. Provider returns success.
6. Your application crashes.
7. Result is never written to PostgreSQL.

After restart, your database still says:

status = IN_PROGRESS

But the payment has already happened.

This is a distributed transaction problem.

You cannot solve it by putting another try/except around the HTTP request.

Three ways to handle it

Option A: Downstream idempotency support

The provider accepts a stable idempotency key.

On retry, submit the identical request using the same key, subject to the provider's documented retention and request-matching rules.

This is usually the simplest approach.

Option B: Query by a stable business reference

If the provider supports transaction lookup, associate the external operation with a stable merchant reference.

When the response is lost:

  1. Query the provider using that reference.
  2. Check whether the transaction exists.
  3. Retrieve its actual status.
  4. Update your local operation ledger.
  5. Only retry when the provider contract establishes that doing so is safe.

Option C: Keep the operation in an unknown state

What happens when the provider doesn't support idempotency and cannot reliably identify the earlier request?

Do not pretend that you can guarantee exactly-once execution.

Keep the operation in UNKNOWN, prevent an automatic duplicate side effect, and route it to reconciliation or human investigation.

This is much safer than charging someone twice because a timeout looked like a failure.

An important distributed-systems rule

The local idempotency ledger protects your application from repeating its own work.

It cannot independently guarantee that a remote system executed a side effect exactly once.

You need a downstream idempotency contract or a reliable reconciliation mechanism.

8. Why an idempotency key alone is not enough

Let's assume you have implemented idempotency keys.

Are you done?

Not yet.

There are several failure modes worth handling explicitly.

Failure 1: The agent uses a new key on retry 

First attempt:
key = payment-001

Second attempt:
key = payment-002

The provider sees two different operations.

Two payments can be created.

Fix: Generate the operation identity in trusted application state and reuse it throughout the workflow.

Failure 2: Same key, different parameters

First request:

{
  "invoice_id": "INV-2048",
  "amount": 480
}

Retry:

{
  "invoice_id": "INV-2048",
  "amount": 840
}

Same key. Different intent.

The system should reject this request.

AWS discusses parameter mismatch handling in its idempotent API design guidance. The IETF's current Idempotency-Key Internet-Draft also defines request fingerprints as a mechanism for detecting this situation.
